questions.title: ROW_NUMBER vs. RANK vs. DENSE_RANK
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in SQL Server. If two products are tied for the highest price, what number does each function give the row right after them?
questions.modelAnswer: All three are ranking window functions used with OVER(ORDER BY ...), and all three number rows based on the order you specify, but they disagree on what happens with ties. ROW_NUMBER() always assigns a unique, sequential integer to every row, even when two rows are tied on the ORDER BY column -- one of the tied rows arbitrarily gets the lower number. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but then skips ahead by the size of the tie: if two rows tie for rank 1, the next distinct row gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() is really counting 'how many rows came before or tied with me, plus one.' DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but the next distinct value gets the very next integer with no gap -- it's counting distinct values, not rows. So for two products tied for the most expensive: ROW_NUMBER gives them 1 and 2 (arbitrarily), RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 3, and DENSE_RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 2.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it with a concrete example because the difference only shows up when there's a tie. Say I'm ranking products by ListPrice and two products are tied for the top price. ROW_NUMBER() doesn't know about ties at all -- it just hands out 1, 2, 3, 4 in order, so the two tied products arbitrarily get 1 and 2. RANK() respects the tie -- both get rank 1 -- but it still 'reserves' a slot for each of them, so the next product down is rank 3, not 2. DENSE_RANK() is the one that feels most natural for something like a pricing tier: both tied products get 1, and the next distinct price is simply 2, no gap. In practice I reach for ROW_NUMBER() constantly for deduplication -- partition by the natural key, order by something like an ID, and anything with RowNum greater than 1 is a duplicate I can delete. I reach for RANK() when ties should genuinely cost a position, like a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for 2nd really does mean nobody is 3rd. And I reach for DENSE_RANK() when I just want the next distinct tier number and don't want gaps confusing anyone reading the report.
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- If two products tie for the top ListPrice:
-- RowNum:     1, 2, 3, 4...  (ties broken arbitrarily)
-- Rank_:      1, 1, 3, 4...  (skips to 3 after the tie)
-- DenseRank_: 1, 1, 2, 3...  (no gap after the tie)
commonMistakes: Saying ROW_NUMBER() can produce duplicate numbers for ties (it never can -- it's always unique)
Mixing up which function skips numbers after a tie (it's RANK, not DENSE_RANK)
Forgetting that ROW_NUMBER() requires ORDER BY inside OVER() -- without it, row order is undefined
Not realizing all three still need PARTITION BY to restart numbering per group
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, ties broken arbitrarily
RANK() gives ties the same number and skips ahead by the tie size afterward
DENSE_RANK() gives ties the same number with no gap for the next distinct value
Choice depends on whether the business question treats a tie as 'costing' a rank

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes ROW_NUMBER's uniqueness behavior
Correctly describes RANK's gap-after-tie behavior
Correctly describes DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over another

questions.title: Transactions: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
questions.prompt: Explain what a transaction is in SQL Server, what COMMIT does that running the statements without a transaction wouldn't, and what exactly ROLLBACK undoes.
questions.modelAnswer: A transaction groups one or more statements into a single all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION marks the start of that group. Until COMMIT runs, the changes are provisional -- visible in the current session but not yet permanently saved, and still subject to being undone. COMMIT TRANSACTION makes every change inside the group permanent, all at once. ROLLBACK TRANSACTION undoes every change made since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION, as if none of it had ever happened. The reason this matters: a multi-step change (like moving stock from one location to another with two separate UPDATE statements) can fail halfway through if run as two independent statements, leaving the data in an inconsistent state. Wrapping both statements in a transaction guarantees either both succeed or neither does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I usually explain this with the classic example: moving inventory from warehouse A to warehouse B is really two UPDATEs -- subtract from A, add to B. If I just run those as two separate statements and the second one fails, I've got stock that's vanished into nowhere. A transaction fixes that by treating both statements as one all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION starts the clock; until I COMMIT, those changes are provisional -- I can see them in my own session, but they're not durably saved and SQL Server can still throw them away. COMMIT makes them permanent. ROLLBACK is the safety net -- if something goes wrong partway through, it undoes everything back to the BEGIN, cleanly, as if I'd never run anything at all. The discipline I bring to it professionally is keeping transactions as short as possible, because every lock held inside one is held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK runs.
commonMistakes: Thinking changes inside a transaction are already permanent before COMMIT runs
Forgetting that ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN TRANSACTION, not just the most recent statement
Leaving a transaction open for a long time, holding locks and blocking other users unnecessarily
Not pairing every BEGIN TRANSACTION with a guaranteed COMMIT or ROLLBACK, even on the error path
keyPoints: A transaction is an all-or-nothing group of statements
Changes are provisional until COMMIT makes them permanent
ROLLBACK undoes everything since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION
Transactions exist to prevent partial, inconsistent multi-step changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a transaction groups together
Correctly explains what COMMIT does and the provisional state before it
Correctly explains the scope of what ROLLBACK undoes
Gives a realistic scenario showing why this matters

questions.title: EXISTS vs. IN vs. JOIN for Existence Checks
questions.prompt: You need to find every customer who has placed at least one order. Compare writing this with EXISTS, with IN, and with an INNER JOIN plus DISTINCT. Explain how each one behaves when a customer has multiple orders, and the specific trap with NOT IN when the subquery's column can contain NULLs.
questions.modelAnswer: EXISTS, IN, and INNER JOIN with DISTINCT can all answer 'does this customer have at least one order,' but they get there differently. EXISTS(subquery) is a pure existence check -- SQL Server can stop scanning the moment it finds one matching row, and a customer with ten orders still only produces one result row, because EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's rows, just a true/false per outer row. IN (subquery) compares the outer column against the whole list the subquery returns; it also naturally avoids duplication since it's testing membership, not joining. An INNER JOIN behaves differently: joining Customer to Order on CustomerID and a customer with three orders produces three joined rows, which means DISTINCT (or GROUP BY) is required afterward to get back to one row per customer -- without it, the result silently overcounts. The sharper trap is with NOT IN rather than IN: if the subquery's column can contain a NULL, NOT IN against that list returns no rows at all for every single outer row, because SQL's three-valued logic can never prove an inequality against an unknown value. EXISTS doesn't have this problem because it's testing a condition, not comparing against a value list, which is one reason NOT EXISTS is generally the safer choice for 'does not have a match.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through why these three roads to the same destination aren't actually equivalent in practice. EXISTS is the one I reach for by default for a pure existence check -- it's a yes/no test, the optimizer can bail out the instant it finds one match, and a customer with ten orders still contributes exactly one row to the result, because EXISTS never pulls the subquery's actual data back. IN behaves similarly for this particular case -- it's checking membership in a list, not joining, so it also doesn't duplicate. Where people get burned is reaching for a plain INNER JOIN instead: the moment you join Customer to Order, a customer with three orders becomes three rows, and if you forget the DISTINCT, you've silently inflated your result set without an error anywhere to tell you. But the real gotcha I always bring up, because it's bitten people in production, is NOT IN with a nullable column -- if even one NULL sneaks into the subquery's result, NOT IN returns completely empty, for every row, with no warning. I treat that as a hard rule: never write NOT IN against a column that could contain NULL -- use NOT EXISTS instead, which doesn't have that failure mode at all.
questions.example:
-- EXISTS: pure existence check, no duplication risk
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM [Order] o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID);

-- IN: membership test against the subquery's result list
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o);

-- JOIN: requires DISTINCT or a customer with 3 orders appears 3 times
SELECT DISTINCT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
INNER JOIN [Order] o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID;

-- THE TRAP: if Order.CustomerID can be NULL, this returns ZERO rows for every customer:
SELECT c.CustomerID FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID NOT IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o); -- avoid if nullable
commonMistakes: Writing a plain INNER JOIN for an existence check and forgetting DISTINCT, silently duplicating customers with multiple orders
Using NOT IN against a subquery column that can contain NULL, not realizing it returns zero rows for every outer row
Assuming EXISTS and IN always perform identically to a JOIN, when EXISTS can short-circuit and avoid materializing the whole list
Not recognizing that EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's column values -- only whether a match exists
keyPoints: EXISTS is a short-circuiting existence check; it returns one result row regardless of how many matches exist
IN compares against a list but doesn't duplicate rows the way a JOIN does
An INNER JOIN needs DISTINCT/GROUP BY to avoid duplicating a row per matching child record
NOT IN against a nullable column can return zero rows entirely -- NOT EXISTS avoids that trap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains EXISTS's existence-check, non-duplicating behavior
Correctly explains why a JOIN needs DISTINCT to avoid duplication
Correctly identifies the NOT IN / NULL trap and why NOT EXISTS avoids it
Provides correct, illustrative SQL for at least two of the three approaches

questions.title: CTEs vs. Views: Same Shape, Different Lifetime
questions.prompt: A coworker says, "I don't get why we need views — a CTE already lets me name a subquery." Explain the real difference between a CTE and a view, and when you'd reach for one over the other.
questions.modelAnswer: A CTE and a view can look nearly identical — both let you name a SELECT and reference it like a table — but they differ in lifetime and scope. A CTE, defined with WITH, exists only for the single statement immediately following it; the moment that statement finishes, the CTE is gone, and no other query, session, or user can reference it. A view, created with CREATE VIEW, is a permanent database object: it's saved once and can be queried by name from any session, any user with permission, indefinitely, until someone runs DROP VIEW. Neither one stores actual data — both re-run their underlying SELECT against live data every time they're referenced. The practical rule: reach for a CTE to make one complex query more readable, especially when you need to reference the same intermediate result twice in that query. Reach for a view when the same logic needs to be reused across many different queries, by many different people or tools, including reporting tools like Power BI connecting directly to the database.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the one-sentence version first: a CTE lives for one statement, a view lives forever until someone deletes it. If I'm writing a gnarly query with three levels of nested subqueries and I just want to name the middle layer so I can read my own logic back, that's a CTE — it's disposable, scoped to right here, right now. But if I've built a 'active customers with more than $1,000 in lifetime orders' query that three different reports are going to need, I don't want three copies of that logic drifting out of sync — I'd save it once as a view, under a clear name, so every query and every person on the team references the same definition. I'd also mention that a view is a real object other tools can see too — if Power BI is connecting directly to the database instead of importing through Power Query, it can query a view exactly like a table, which a CTE could never support.
questions.example:
-- CTE: scoped to this one statement only
WITH RecentOrders AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, SUM(TotalDue) AS Total
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
    WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01'
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT * FROM RecentOrders WHERE Total > 5000;
-- RecentOrders no longer exists after this statement runs.

-- View: saved permanently, reusable by anyone with access
CREATE VIEW vw_RecentOrderTotals AS
SELECT CustomerID, SUM(TotalDue) AS Total
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01'
GROUP BY CustomerID;

SELECT * FROM vw_RecentOrderTotals WHERE Total > 5000;
commonMistakes: Assuming a CTE can be reused across multiple separate statements or sessions (it can't)
Assuming either one stores a physical copy of the data (both re-run their SELECT live)
Reaching for a view for a one-off readability fix inside a single complex query, when a CTE is simpler and doesn't leave a permanent object behind
Forgetting that a view is directly queryable by reporting tools connecting to the database, the way a CTE never could be
keyPoints: A CTE is scoped to one statement; a view persists until explicitly dropped
Neither stores data — both run their SELECT fresh against live data each time
CTEs suit one-off readability inside a single complex query
Views suit logic that needs to be reused across many queries, people, or tools

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains a CTE's one-statement lifetime
Correctly explains a view's persistent, reusable lifetime
States that neither stores data, both re-run live
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over the other

questions.title: What Makes a Window Function Different from GROUP BY
questions.prompt: Explain how a window function using OVER() differs from GROUP BY, and why you might reach for AVG(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) instead of a GROUP BY query, even though both compute an average per category.
questions.modelAnswer: GROUP BY and a window function can compute the exact same aggregate — an average per category — but they do fundamentally different things to the result set. GROUP BY collapses every row in a group down into a single summary row, so a table of 500 products grouped by category becomes a handful of rows, one per category, with the individual products gone. A window function, triggered by adding OVER() to an aggregate, computes the same aggregate across a group of related rows but keeps every original row intact in the output — nothing collapses. PARTITION BY inside OVER() divides rows into groups purely for that calculation's purpose, exactly like GROUP BY divides rows, but the row-level result is untouched. The practical reason to reach for the window function version: you need the category average sitting alongside each individual product's own price, for example to compute how far above or below that category's average a specific product is priced — a comparison GROUP BY's collapsed output couldn't support at all, since the individual product's own price no longer exists in a grouped result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with what actually happens to the rows, because that's the real distinction, not just syntax. GROUP BY by category gives me one row per category — Bikes, Accessories, Clothing — and the individual products are gone from the output. AVG(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) gives me back every single product row, but now each one also carries its own category's average price as an extra column sitting right next to it. That's the whole reason I'd reach for the window function version: I usually want to compare something at the row level against a group-level number — 'how does this specific product's price compare to the average for its category?' — and I can only do that math if both numbers are available on the same row. If all I actually need is the category averages themselves, with no individual rows attached, plain GROUP BY is simpler and I wouldn't bother with OVER() at all.
questions.example:
-- GROUP BY: collapses to one row per category
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, AVG(ListPrice) AS AvgPrice
FROM Production.Product
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;

-- Window function: keeps every product row, adds the category average alongside it
SELECT Name, ProductSubcategoryID, ListPrice,
       AVG(ListPrice) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductSubcategoryID) AS AvgPriceForCategory,
       ListPrice - AVG(ListPrice) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductSubcategoryID) AS DiffFromAvg
FROM Production.Product;
commonMistakes: Saying GROUP BY and a window function always return the same number of rows (GROUP BY collapses; a window function does not)
Forgetting PARTITION BY is required to restart the calculation per group, not just ORDER BY
Assuming a window function requires an aggregate you can't also compute with GROUP BY — the aggregate itself is identical, only the row-collapsing behavior differs
Using GROUP BY when the goal was actually a row-level comparison against a group total, then wondering why the individual values disappeared
keyPoints: GROUP BY collapses rows into one summary row per group
A window function (OVER()) keeps every original row while still computing a per-group aggregate
PARTITION BY divides rows into groups for the window calculation only, without collapsing anything
Choose the window function when you need a row-level value compared against a group-level aggregate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains GROUP BY's row-collapsing behavior
Correctly explains that a window function preserves every row
Correctly describes PARTITION BY's role
Gives a realistic scenario where the window function's row-level detail matters

questions.title: Azure SQL Database vs. Managed Instance vs. SQL Server on a VM
questions.prompt: A company wants to move an on-prem SQL Server instance to Azure. Explain the real differences between Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and SQL Server on an Azure VM, and what would push a decision toward each one.
questions.modelAnswer: The three options trade off management overhead against compatibility and control, and they sit on a spectrum rather than being three unrelated products. Azure SQL Database is a fully managed PaaS single database (or elastic pool) -- Microsoft handles the OS, patching, and most instance-level configuration, but it doesn't expose full SQL Server instance-level surface area (no SQL Agent in the classic sense, no cross-database queries, no instance-level DMVs covering multiple databases). Azure SQL Managed Instance is also PaaS, but it emulates a nearly complete SQL Server instance -- cross-database queries, SQL Agent, linked servers, and most instance-level features work, at the cost of slightly more deployment overhead (it needs a dedicated subnet) and a higher baseline cost. SQL Server on an Azure VM is IaaS -- it's just SQL Server running on a VM you manage yourself, giving 100% feature parity with on-prem SQL Server (every version, every feature, full OS access) at the cost of the customer being responsible for patching, backups, and HA/DR configuration themselves. The decision rule: choose Azure SQL Database for a single modern application that doesn't need instance-level features and wants the least operational burden; choose Managed Instance when migrating an existing multi-database application that relies on SQL Agent, cross-database queries, or linked servers, but still wants PaaS-level patching; choose a VM when something needs a specific SQL Server version/feature/third-party integration that only works with full instance and OS access.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as a spectrum from least to most control, because that's really what's being traded. Azure SQL Database is the fully hands-off end -- Microsoft patches it, manages the OS, and you just connect to a database -- but it doesn't give you a full instance, so no cross-database queries and no classic SQL Agent. If an app is a single, fairly self-contained database, that's usually the right default. Managed Instance sits in the middle -- it's still PaaS, Microsoft still patches it, but it behaves like a real SQL Server instance: SQL Agent works, cross-database queries work, linked servers work. I reach for that specifically when I'm migrating something that already depends on instance-level features and I don't want to rewrite the application just to fit the Database tier's constraints. SQL Server on a VM is the other end -- full control, full compatibility, but now patching, backup strategy, and HA/DR are entirely on us to configure and maintain, the same as on-prem. In an interview I'd always tie the choice back to what the existing application actually needs rather than defaulting to 'VM because it's most flexible,' since that flexibility comes with real operational cost.
commonMistakes: Assuming Azure SQL Database supports cross-database queries and SQL Agent the same way a full instance does
Choosing a VM by default for 'maximum flexibility' without weighing the ongoing patching and HA/DR burden that comes with it
Not recognizing Managed Instance needs its own dedicated subnet, which affects network planning
Treating the three options as interchangeable rather than a genuine compatibility-vs-management tradeoff
keyPoints: Azure SQL Database: fully managed single database/elastic pool, least overhead, no full instance surface
Managed Instance: PaaS with near-complete instance compatibility (SQL Agent, cross-database queries, linked servers)
SQL Server on a VM: full IaaS control and compatibility, but customer owns patching and HA/DR
The decision should be driven by what the existing or planned application actually requires

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Azure SQL Database's management model and limitations
Correctly distinguishes Managed Instance's near-full compatibility
Correctly distinguishes the VM option's full control and operational burden
Gives a reasoned decision rule tied to application needs

lessonLink.label: Review: Azure SQL Database vs. Managed Instance vs. SQL Server on Azure VM

questions.title: DTU vs. vCore: What's Actually Being Purchased
questions.prompt: A teammate asks why Azure SQL Database offers both a DTU-based and a vCore-based purchasing model instead of just one. Explain the real difference between them and when vCore is the clearly better choice.
questions.modelAnswer: The DTU model bundles CPU, memory, and I/O into a single blended unit (a Database Transaction Unit) and a database is purchased as a tier (Basic, Standard, Premium) with a DTU count -- it's simple to reason about but opaque about which specific resource is actually the bottleneck, and it doesn't let you scale CPU and memory independently of each other. The vCore model instead lets you specify actual CPU cores and a memory ratio directly, mirroring how on-prem licensing and sizing normally works, and it supports Azure Hybrid Benefit, letting a customer apply an existing SQL Server license toward the Azure bill at a real discount -- something the DTU model doesn't offer at all. vCore is the clearly better choice whenever the customer has existing SQL Server licenses to apply (Hybrid Benefit alone can be a large cost difference), whenever precise, independent control over compute and memory matters for a demanding or well-understood workload, or whenever straightforward cost transparency tied to actual hardware resources is wanted instead of an abstracted DTU number.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain DTU as the simpler, bundled option -- one number that blends CPU, memory, and I/O together into a tier, which is easy to pick off a chart but genuinely opaque once something's actually struggling, because the DTU number alone doesn't tell you whether you're CPU-bound, memory-bound, or I/O-bound. vCore unbundles that -- you pick actual cores and a memory tier, much closer to how an on-prem DBA already thinks about sizing a server. The detail I'd always bring up first in an interview, because it's the single biggest real-world reason to pick vCore, is Azure Hybrid Benefit: if the customer already owns SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance, vCore lets them apply those licenses against the Azure cost, which can be a substantial discount that the DTU model simply has no equivalent for. So in practice, unless it's a very small, simple workload where DTU's bundled simplicity genuinely doesn't matter, I default to recommending vCore, especially the moment existing licensing is in the picture.
commonMistakes: Describing DTU and vCore as just two different billing units with no functional difference
Forgetting that Azure Hybrid Benefit is only available under the vCore model, not DTU
Assuming DTU is always cheaper for small workloads without actually comparing the equivalent vCore configuration
Not recognizing that DTU bundles CPU/memory/I/O while vCore allows independent sizing of compute and memory
keyPoints: DTU bundles CPU, memory, and I/O into one blended unit per service tier
vCore lets you specify actual cores and memory independently, closer to on-prem sizing
Azure Hybrid Benefit (applying existing SQL Server licenses) is only available under vCore
vCore is the clearly better choice once existing licensing or precise resource control matters

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the DTU model's bundled, blended-unit nature
Correctly explains the vCore model's independent compute/memory sizing
Correctly identifies Azure Hybrid Benefit as a vCore-only advantage
Gives a reasoned scenario for when vCore is clearly the better choice

lessonLink.label: Review: DTU vs. vCore & Choosing the Right Database Configuration

questions.title: SQL Authentication vs. Microsoft Entra Authentication
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between SQL Authentication and Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) Authentication for Azure SQL, and why a security-conscious DBA would push to minimize SQL logins in favor of Entra authentication wherever possible.
questions.modelAnswer: SQL Authentication relies on a username and password stored and validated inside SQL Server itself -- the credential is a standalone secret with no connection to any broader identity system, meaning it has to be manually rotated, manually disabled when someone leaves, and is only as strong as whatever password policy is enforced at creation. Microsoft Entra Authentication instead validates identity against Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), the same identity system used for the rest of the organization's Microsoft 365 and Azure resources -- a user logs in with their actual organizational identity, inheriting conditional access policies, MFA enforcement, and centralized lifecycle management (when someone's Entra account is disabled, their database access is effectively disabled too, with no separate step). A security-conscious DBA minimizes SQL logins because they're a standing, disconnected credential that outlives employment changes unless someone remembers to clean it up, can't enforce MFA on its own, and represents one more secret that has to be tracked and rotated manually -- versus Entra authentication, where access follows the same centralized identity lifecycle as everything else the organization manages.
questions.professionalAnswer: The practical difference I'd lead with is where the credential actually lives. SQL Authentication's password lives and is checked entirely inside SQL Server -- it's disconnected from everything else, so when someone leaves the company, unless I specifically remember to go disable that SQL login, it just keeps working. Entra Authentication ties the login to the person's actual organizational identity, so it inherits MFA, conditional access, and -- critically -- gets disabled automatically the moment IT disables their Entra account for any other reason, because it's the same identity, not a separate one I have to remember to manage. That's the real argument for pushing Entra authentication as the default: it's not just 'more modern,' it closes a specific, common gap where a departed employee's database access silently survives because a SQL login was never part of the offboarding checklist. I still keep a small number of SQL logins around for specific cases -- a legacy app that genuinely can't do Entra auth, or a break-glass admin account -- but I treat each one as a deliberate exception I can justify, not the default.
commonMistakes: Treating SQL Authentication and Entra Authentication as equally secure options with no real tradeoff
Forgetting that a disabled Entra account automatically loses database access, while a SQL login requires a separate manual step
Not mentioning that Entra authentication inherits MFA and conditional access policies, which SQL logins cannot enforce on their own
Treating 'minimize SQL logins' as 'eliminate them entirely' without acknowledging legitimate exceptions like legacy apps
keyPoints: SQL Authentication stores and validates credentials entirely within SQL Server, disconnected from any other identity system
Entra Authentication ties access to the organization's actual identity system, inheriting MFA and conditional access
An offboarded employee's Entra-based access is cut automatically; a SQL login requires a separate manual step
SQL logins should be a deliberate, justified exception, not the default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains where each authentication type's credential actually lives
Correctly explains the MFA/conditional-access inheritance advantage of Entra auth
Correctly explains the offboarding/lifecycle advantage of Entra auth
Acknowledges legitimate remaining use cases for SQL logins

lessonLink.label: Review: SQL Authentication vs. Microsoft Entra Authentication

questions.title: What Transparent Data Encryption Actually Protects
questions.prompt: A manager asks whether enabling Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) on an Azure SQL Database means data sent to a reporting tool is now encrypted in transit. Explain exactly what TDE protects, and what it does not.
questions.modelAnswer: TDE encrypts data at rest -- the physical database files, log files, and backups -- so that if someone obtained a raw copy of those files (a stolen backup, a disk image) without valid credentials, the contents would be unreadable without the encryption key. It does this transparently to applications: queries, connections, and tools interact with the database exactly as before, with no application code changes required, because the encryption/decryption happens at the storage engine level. Critically, TDE does nothing for data once it leaves the storage layer -- a query result returned to a reporting tool, or data flowing over a network connection, is not protected by TDE at all; that's a separate concern handled by Transport Layer Security (encryption in transit) and is on by default for Azure SQL connections, but it's a distinct mechanism from TDE. TDE is also not a substitute for access control -- anyone with valid database permissions can query and see plaintext data exactly as before; TDE only protects against someone bypassing the database engine entirely and reading the raw files directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct the specific misunderstanding directly: TDE is about data at rest, not data in transit, and those are genuinely two separate protections. What TDE actually does is encrypt the physical database and log files and backups on disk, so if someone somehow got their hands on a raw backup file or a disk image without the right key, it would just be unreadable noise to them -- but anyone querying the database normally, with valid credentials, sees completely normal, readable data, because TDE is transparent to the query layer by design. Data moving to a reporting tool over the network is protected by TLS, a separate mechanism that's on by default for Azure SQL connections -- TDE has nothing to do with that leg of the trip at all. I'd also be clear that TDE isn't an access-control mechanism -- it doesn't stop a user with legitimate database permissions from seeing the data; it protects specifically against someone bypassing the database entirely and grabbing the raw files off storage or out of a backup.
commonMistakes: Assuming TDE encrypts data in transit between the database and a client or reporting tool
Believing TDE prevents a user with valid database permissions from seeing plaintext data
Thinking TDE requires application-level code changes, when it operates transparently at the storage engine
Confusing TDE with Always Encrypted, which does protect specific column data even from a DBA with database access
keyPoints: TDE encrypts data at rest: database files, log files, and backups
TDE is transparent -- no application changes required, queries behave normally
Data in transit is protected separately by TLS, not by TDE
TDE doesn't restrict what a user with valid database permissions can see

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that TDE protects data at rest specifically
Correctly clarifies that data in transit is a separate concern (TLS)
Correctly explains TDE doesn't restrict normal query access for valid users
Communicates the distinction clearly for a non-technical manager

questions.title: Server-Level vs. Database-Level Firewall Rules
questions.prompt: Azure SQL supports both server-level and database-level firewall rules. Explain the difference, and a real scenario where only a database-level rule is the right tool.
questions.modelAnswer: A server-level firewall rule is defined once on the logical SQL server and applies to every database hosted under it -- an IP range allowed at the server level can reach any database on that server, assuming the right credentials. A database-level firewall rule is scoped to a single specific database and is actually stored inside that database itself (which matters for geo-replication and failover, since the rule travels with the database). The real scenario for a database-level rule: a multi-tenant setup where one server hosts databases for several different clients, and one client's application needs access from an IP range that shouldn't automatically be able to reach every other client's database on the same server -- a server-level rule would grant that IP blanket access to everything on the server, while a database-level rule scopes it precisely to just that one client's database.
questions.professionalAnswer: The distinction is really about blast radius. A server-level rule lives on the logical server and quietly opens that IP range to every database hosted there -- convenient, but it's an all-or-nothing grant across however many databases that server has. A database-level rule is scoped to one specific database, and it actually lives inside that database's own metadata, which has a nice side effect: if that database fails over as part of geo-replication, the rule travels with it instead of being left behind on the old server. The scenario where I'd insist on database-level specifically is multi-tenant hosting -- say one Azure SQL server hosts five different clients' databases to save cost, and client A's office IP needs access. A server-level rule for that IP would hand client A's network blanket reachability to clients B through E's databases too, which is exactly the kind of over-broad access a security review would flag. A database-level rule scoped to just client A's database closes that gap entirely.
commonMistakes: Assuming a server-level rule only grants access to one database
Not realizing a database-level rule is stored with the database itself and travels with it on failover
Defaulting to server-level rules for convenience without considering the broader access they grant
Forgetting that both rule types still require valid authentication -- the firewall is a network gate, not an authorization mechanism
keyPoints: A server-level rule grants an IP range access to every database on that logical server
A database-level rule scopes access to one specific database, and travels with it on failover
Database-level rules are the right tool for multi-tenant hosting where blast radius matters
Firewall rules control network reachability, not authorization -- valid credentials are still required

Correctly explains that database-level rules travel with the database on failover
Gives a realistic, correct scenario where database-level is the right choice
Clarifies firewall rules control network access, not authorization

questions.title: Reading sys.dm_db_missing_index_details Correctly
questions.prompt: Explain what sys.dm_db_missing_index_details actually tells you, and why blindly creating every index it suggests is a bad idea.
questions.modelAnswer: sys.dm_db_missing_index_details is a dynamic management view that records index suggestions the query optimizer noticed it could have used, based on queries that have actually run since the last SQL Server restart -- it reports which columns would help as equality predicates, inequality predicates, and included columns, along with related DMVs (sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups and sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats) that estimate how much it might have helped and how often the opportunity came up. The reason it's dangerous to blindly implement every suggestion: the view has no awareness of indexes that already exist and might overlap heavily with a suggestion, no awareness of how many other indexes already exist on that table (every additional index slows down inserts/updates/deletes, since each one needs maintaining), and it reports raw counts that reset on a service restart, so a suggestion that looks heavily used might just reflect activity since the last restart rather than genuine ongoing need. A responsible approach treats these as a starting hypothesis to investigate -- checking for overlap with existing indexes, weighing the suggestion against the table's actual write load -- rather than a checklist to apply mechanically.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat sys.dm_db_missing_index_details exactly as its name implies -- a list of things the optimizer noticed it was missing while running real queries, not a prescription to follow blindly. It tells you the columns that would help, split into equality, inequality, and included columns, and the related stats view gives you a rough sense of potential impact and how often the pattern showed up. The trap people fall into is treating every row as an index to create immediately. In practice I always check it against what indexes already exist on that table first, because the DMV has no idea an index covering 90% of the same need might already be sitting there -- creating a near-duplicate just adds write overhead for marginal gain. I also remember these counters reset on every SQL Server restart, so a huge-looking impact number might just mean the server restarted recently and that one query pattern happened to run a lot since then, not that it's been a chronic, years-long gap. My actual workflow is: pull the suggestions, cross-reference existing indexes, check Query Store or the plan cache for how often the pattern genuinely recurs, and only then decide whether a new index earns its ongoing write-cost tax.
questions.example:
-- Find missing index suggestions with their estimated impact
SELECT mid.statement AS TableName,
       mid.equality_columns,
       mid.inequality_columns,
       mid.included_columns,
       migs.avg_user_impact,
       migs.user_seeks
FROM sys.dm_db_missing_index_details mid
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups mig ON mid.index_handle = mig.index_handle
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats migs ON mig.index_group_handle = migs.group_handle
ORDER BY migs.avg_user_impact * migs.user_seeks DESC;
commonMistakes: Creating every suggested index mechanically without checking for overlap with existing indexes
Treating the impact/usage numbers as lifetime totals rather than counts since the last SQL Server restart
Not weighing the write-overhead cost of a new index against its read benefit
Ignoring that the DMV only reports on queries that have actually run, missing patterns that haven't executed recently
keyPoints: sys.dm_db_missing_index_details reports columns the optimizer noticed could have used an index, based on actual executed queries
Related DMVs estimate potential impact and how often the opportunity recurred
Counters reset on service restart, so impact numbers reflect recent activity, not lifetime history
Every suggestion should be cross-checked against existing indexes and write-cost before creating it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what sys.dm_db_missing_index_details reports
Correctly explains the overlap-with-existing-indexes risk
Correctly explains the restart-reset caveat on the stats
Provides correct, relevant example SQL

questions.title: What Query Store Actually Captures
questions.prompt: Explain what Query Store captures that the plan cache alone doesn't, and why that makes it specifically useful for diagnosing a query that got slower after a deployment.
questions.modelAnswer: The plan cache only holds the current execution plan for a query, and it's volatile -- a plan can be evicted under memory pressure, or replaced the moment the query recompiles with a new plan, at which point the old plan and its performance history are simply gone. Query Store instead persistently records query text, multiple execution plans a query has had over time, and runtime statistics (duration, CPU, I/O, execution count) bucketed into time intervals, specifically so that history survives recompiles, plan cache evictions, and even server restarts. This is exactly what makes it the right tool for 'this query got slower after a deployment' -- Query Store lets you look at the same query's performance over a time window spanning before and after the deployment, see whether a different plan was chosen (a plan regression), and even force the prior, better-performing plan back on if that turns out to be the cause, all without the plan cache's volatility destroying the evidence you'd need to diagnose it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The plan cache is a snapshot of right now -- whatever plan is currently cached, which can vanish the instant memory pressure evicts it or the query recompiles with a different plan, taking its performance history with it. Query Store is built specifically to survive that: it persists query text, every distinct plan a query has actually used over time, and runtime stats bucketed into intervals, so none of that disappears on a recompile or even a restart. That's exactly why it's my first stop for 'this got slower after we deployed something' -- I can pull up the same query's history spanning before and after the deployment date, and Query Store will often show me directly that the optimizer picked a different, worse plan right around that time, which is a plan regression, not some vague 'the server is slow' mystery. The feature that makes this genuinely actionable rather than just diagnostic is that I can force the old, better plan back on directly from Query Store while the real fix (an index, a statistics update, a query rewrite) gets planned properly, instead of being stuck either living with the regression or guessing at a fix under pressure.
commonMistakes: Assuming the plan cache retains the same historical detail that Query Store provides
Not recognizing that a plan can change (regress) without any code change, just from a statistics update or a recompile
Forgetting Query Store can force a previous plan directly, offering an immediate mitigation separate from the root-cause fix
Treating Query Store purely as a reporting tool rather than an actionable regression-diagnosis tool
keyPoints: The plan cache is volatile -- it can be evicted or replaced, losing history
Query Store persistently records query text, multiple plans over time, and bucketed runtime stats
This makes it possible to compare a query's performance before and after a specific change
Query Store can force a previous plan back on as an immediate mitigation for a regression

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the plan cache's volatility and limitations
Correctly explains what Query Store persistently captures
Correctly ties this to diagnosing a post-deployment regression
Mentions forcing a previous plan as an available mitigation

questions.title: Failover Groups vs. Active Geo-Replication
questions.prompt: Azure SQL offers both Active Geo-Replication and Auto-Failover Groups. Explain the real difference between them, given that a failover group is built on top of geo-replication rather than replacing it.
questions.modelAnswer: Active Geo-Replication creates up to four readable secondary replicas of a database in different regions, continuously replicating data -- it's the underlying replication technology, and failing over to a secondary is a manual operation the DBA has to initiate, which also means the application's connection string has to be manually updated to point at the new primary. An Auto-Failover Group is built on top of geo-replication for exactly one primary-secondary pair, adding two things geo-replication alone doesn't have: a stable listener endpoint (a DNS name that always points at whichever database is currently primary, so the application's connection string never has to change) and automatic failover based on configurable health-detection policies, so the group can fail over without a human manually triggering it. The practical implication: if an application needs multiple readable secondaries across several regions, geo-replication (without a failover group, or with one wrapping just the DR pair) is still the mechanism; if the goal is 'the application doesn't need to know or care which region is currently primary, and failover should happen automatically during a regional outage,' a failover group is the layer that actually delivers that.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as two layers, not two competing technologies. Geo-replication is the actual replication mechanism -- it's what continuously copies the database to up to four secondaries in other regions, and those secondaries are readable the whole time. But geo-replication by itself leaves two gaps: failing over is a manual action I have to trigger, and the application's connection string has to point at a specific server name, which changes when I fail over. A failover group sits on top of exactly one geo-replication pair and closes both gaps -- it gives me a listener endpoint, a stable DNS name the application always connects to regardless of which side is currently primary, and it can detect an outage and fail over automatically based on a policy I configure, instead of me having to be awake and watching. So if someone needs several read replicas spread across regions for reporting, that's geo-replication doing its normal job. If the actual requirement is 'the app shouldn't need a manual connection-string change during a regional disaster, and ideally failover happens without someone paged at 3 AM,' that's specifically what a failover group adds on top.
commonMistakes: Treating Active Geo-Replication and Auto-Failover Groups as two unrelated, competing features
Assuming geo-replication alone provides automatic failover without a failover group layered on top
Forgetting that a failover group provides a stable listener endpoint, removing the need to update connection strings
Not recognizing geo-replication supports up to four secondaries, while a failover group wraps just one primary-secondary pair
keyPoints: Active Geo-Replication is the underlying replication mechanism, supporting up to four readable secondaries
Geo-replication alone requires manual failover and a manual connection-string update
A failover group adds a stable listener endpoint and automatic, policy-based failover on top of one geo-replication pair
The choice depends on whether multiple read replicas or hands-off automatic failover is the actual goal

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what Active Geo-Replication provides on its own
Correctly explains what a failover group adds on top of geo-replication
Correctly frames the failover group as built on, not a replacement for, geo-replication
Gives a clear scenario distinguishing when each is the right tool

questions.title: Top-2-per-group with a window function
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product table that returns the two highest-priced products in each color, without using a correlated subquery.
questions.modelAnswer: The idiomatic way to solve 'top N per group' in T-SQL is PARTITION BY plus ROW_NUMBER(), wrapped in a CTE so the ranking column can be filtered afterward. PARTITION BY Color restarts the numbering at 1 for each color, and ORDER BY ListPrice DESC makes 1 the most expensive product in that color. You can't filter directly on ROW_NUMBER() in the same SELECT's WHERE clause because window functions are logically evaluated after WHERE -- that's why the CTE (or a subquery) is necessary.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'top N per group' problem, and the pattern I reach for every time is a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by the grouping column. I avoid a correlated subquery with TOP 2 inside it because that approach re-executes once per outer row and doesn't scale well. Instead, I compute the rank once in a CTE, then just filter WHERE RankInColor <= 2 in the outer query. The one gotcha I always mention out loud in an interview: you cannot write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= 2 directly in the same SELECT, because the WHERE clause is logically evaluated before window functions are computed -- that's exactly why the CTE wrapper is required, not just a style preference.
questions.example:
WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Color ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RankInColor
    FROM Production.Product
)
SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice
FROM Ranked
WHERE RankInColor <= 2
ORDER BY Color, RankInColor;
-- The CTE is required because ROW_NUMBER() can't be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE clause.
commonMistakes: Trying to filter WHERE ROW_NUMBER() <= 2 directly in the same SELECT (not legal -- window functions evaluate after WHERE)
Forgetting PARTITION BY and ranking across the whole table instead of per color
Using TOP 2 with a correlated subquery per group, which is correct but far less efficient on large tables
Omitting ORDER BY inside OVER(), which leaves 'top' undefined
keyPoints: PARTITION BY restarts the ranking per group (per color here)
A CTE or subquery is required to filter on the window function's result
ORDER BY DESC inside OVER() makes rank 1 the highest price
This pattern generalizes to any 'top N per group' business question

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses ROW_NUMBER() with correct PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
Wraps it in a CTE/subquery to filter correctly
Query is syntactically valid and returns exactly 2 rows per color
Explains why filtering can't happen in the same SELECT's WHERE clause

questions.title: Temp table, table variable, or CTE?
questions.prompt: You need to hold an intermediate result set of about 500,000 rows, reuse it across three separate statements in a stored procedure, and would benefit from adding your own index to it. Which of #temp table, @table variable, or CTE would you choose, and why would the other two be worse choices here?
questions.modelAnswer: A #temp table is the right choice. It's a real, physically-stored table in tempdb, so SQL Server maintains real statistics on it (row counts), which lets the optimizer build a much smarter plan for a large result set, and you can explicitly add your own indexes to it. A table variable would be the wrong choice here: it also lives in tempdb, but historically has no maintained statistics, so on older compatibility levels the optimizer may assume just one row and badly under-allocate resources for 500,000 rows -- and while you can add inline PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE constraints, you can't add arbitrary indexes the way you can on a #temp table. A CTE would also be the wrong choice: it isn't physically stored at all -- it's inlined into the query -- so referencing it in three separate statements could mean SQL Server re-runs its underlying query multiple times, and you can't add an index to something that was never materialized.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given the three constraints in the question -- large row count, reused across multiple statements, and wanting an index -- a #temp table wins on all three. The decision rule I use: CTEs are for one-time readability or recursion, not for reuse -- a CTE doesn't store anything, it's re-inlined at every reference, so touching it from three separate statements risks the underlying query running three separate times. Table variables are for small result sets inside a procedure where I want to avoid plan recompiles -- but historically they carry no real statistics, so the optimizer can badly misjudge a large one. A #temp table is the one option that's physically stored with real statistics the optimizer can use, and the only one of the three where I can explicitly add an index after the fact. For 500,000 rows reused three times, I'm reaching for #temp every time.
commonMistakes: Choosing a CTE for something reused across multiple statements, not realizing it may re-run its query each time
Choosing a table variable for a large result set, assuming it always performs the same as a temp table
Not mentioning that #temp tables maintain real statistics while table variables historically don't
Forgetting that CTEs can't be indexed at all, since nothing is actually materialized
keyPoints: #Temp tables are physically stored with maintained statistics and can be indexed
Table variables historically lack statistics, risking a poor plan on large sets
CTEs are inlined, not stored, and may re-execute their query on every reference
Choice depends on size, reuse, and whether an index is needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly chooses the #temp table for this scenario
Correctly explains why a table variable would be worse here
Correctly explains why a CTE would be worse here
Provides valid, relevant example code

questions.title: Raising a custom business-rule error
questions.prompt: Write T-SQL that checks whether a discount percentage exceeds 50% and, if so, raises a custom error using the modern recommended syntax. Then show how you would log an error inside a CATCH block and still let it propagate to the caller.
questions.modelAnswer: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error, taking an error number, a message, and a state, and raising it exactly as if SQL Server had generated it itself. For a business rule like a discount cap, you check the condition and THROW a custom error if it's violated. To log an error and still propagate it, use THROW with no arguments inside a CATCH block -- it re-raises the exact error that was just caught, unmodified, after whatever logging or cleanup logic runs first. RAISERROR is the older syntax, still common in existing code, with a different argument shape (message, severity, state) -- recognize it, but prefer THROW for new code.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the business rule check itself, I'd write a simple IF that tests the discount, and THROW a custom error number with a clear message if it's violated -- that's the modern, recommended way, and it's a one-liner. The more interesting half of this question is re-throwing from a CATCH block, because that's a pattern people often get wrong: they either swallow the error silently after logging it, or they try to reconstruct it with a new THROW statement and lose the original error details. The clean way is TRY/CATCH around the risky operation, log whatever you need to inside CATCH, and then just write THROW with no arguments -- that re-raises the exact error that was caught, unmodified, so the caller still sees the real failure instead of a sanitized stand-in.
questions.example:
-- Business rule check
IF @DiscountPercent > 50
    THROW 50000, 'Discount cannot exceed 50 percent.', 1;

-- Logging then re-throwing the original error
BEGIN TRY
    UPDATE Sales.SpecialOffer SET DiscountPct = @DiscountPercent WHERE SpecialOfferID = @ID;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    INSERT INTO ErrorLog (ErrorMessage, LoggedAt) VALUES (ERROR_MESSAGE(), GETDATE());
    THROW; -- re-raises the exact caught error, unmodified
END CATCH
commonMistakes: Using RAISERROR for new code instead of the modern, recommended THROW
Writing a new THROW statement inside CATCH instead of bare THROW, which loses the original error's details
Forgetting THROW's argument order is (error number, message, state) -- a different shape than RAISERROR's
Swallowing the error entirely after logging it, instead of re-throwing so the caller knows it failed
keyPoints: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error
Bare THROW inside CATCH re-raises the exact original error
RAISERROR is the older syntax, still seen in legacy code
Logging an error doesn't have to mean swallowing it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses THROW to raise a custom business-rule error
Correctly uses TRY/CATCH with bare THROW to re-raise after logging
Explains the difference between THROW and RAISERROR
Code is syntactically valid T-SQL

questions.title: Join Four Tables, Mixing INNER and LEFT
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012 that returns each order line's product name, order date, and the customer's first and last name, including order lines for products that may no longer have a subcategory assigned. Use at least one LEFT JOIN alongside INNER JOINs.
questions.modelAnswer: This requires chaining four tables together: SalesOrderHeader (for the order date and customer link), SalesOrderDetail (the order lines), Product (for the product name), and Person (for the customer's name), while also reaching ProductSubcategory with a LEFT JOIN so that products missing a subcategory still appear instead of being silently excluded. Each JOIN connects to whatever table already has the needed column available, not necessarily the very first table named in FROM — for instance, the join to Product uses ProductID from SalesOrderDetail, introduced by the join just before it. The LEFT JOIN to ProductSubcategory is the one deliberate choice: an INNER JOIN there would drop any order line whose product has a NULL ProductSubcategoryID, which is exactly the scenario the question asks to preserve.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this one join at a time rather than writing the whole thing at once, because that's the only way to keep four tables straight. I start from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail joined on SalesOrderID, since that's the backbone of the query. Then I bring in Product on ProductID to get the product name, and Person on CustomerID (really BusinessEntityID) to get the name. All three of those are INNER JOINs because I genuinely need a match on all of them for the row to make sense. The one place I'd stop and think is ProductSubcategory — the question specifically says some products might not have one, and an INNER JOIN there would quietly drop those order lines from the result with no warning. That's exactly the signal to use LEFT JOIN instead, so a product with a NULL ProductSubcategoryID still shows up, just with NULL in the subcategory column rather than vanishing from the report entirely.
questions.example:
SELECT soh.OrderDate, p.Name AS ProductName, per.FirstName, per.LastName, ps.Name AS SubcategoryName
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader AS soh
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON soh.SalesOrderID = sod.SalesOrderID
INNER JOIN Production.Product AS p
    ON sod.ProductID = p.ProductID
INNER JOIN Person.Person AS per
    ON soh.CustomerID = per.BusinessEntityID
LEFT JOIN Production.ProductSubcategory AS ps
    ON p.ProductSubcategoryID = ps.ProductSubcategoryID;
commonMistakes: Using INNER JOIN on ProductSubcategory, which silently drops any order line for a product missing a subcategory
Joining to the wrong table's column (e.g. trying to reach ProductID directly from SalesOrderHeader, which doesn't have it)
Forgetting table aliases on a four-table query, making it unreadable and error-prone to debug
Not noticing that CustomerID on SalesOrderHeader maps to BusinessEntityID on Person.Person, not a column literally named CustomerID there
keyPoints: Each JOIN can reference any table already available earlier in the query, not just the first one
LEFT JOIN preserves rows that would otherwise be dropped by a stricter INNER JOIN
Mixing INNER and LEFT JOIN in one query is normal when different relationships have different guarantees
Clear aliases are essential once a query joins more than two or three tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly joins all four required tables
Uses LEFT JOIN specifically for ProductSubcategory
Query is syntactically valid and returns the correct columns
Explains why LEFT JOIN was chosen there instead of INNER JOIN

questions.title: Creating a Database-Scoped Firewall Rule in T-SQL
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL to create a database-level firewall rule allowing the IP range 203.0.113.10 through 203.0.113.20 to reach a specific Azure SQL database, and explain which database you must be connected to when you run it.
questions.modelAnswer: A database-level firewall rule is created with sp_set_database_firewall_rule, specifying a rule name and the start and end IP of the allowed range. The critical detail is that this stored procedure must be run while connected directly to the specific database the rule should apply to, not the master database -- a database-level rule is stored inside that database itself, so running it against the wrong database creates a rule scoped to the wrong place, or fails outright depending on permissions. This is different from a server-level rule, created with sp_set_firewall_rule, which must be run against the master database instead.
questions.professionalAnswer: The call itself is simple: EXEC sp_set_database_firewall_rule with a rule name and the start/end IP range. The part people get wrong is the connection context -- I have to be connected directly to the target database, not master, because this rule lives inside that specific database and travels with it if it's ever geo-replicated or failed over. If I ran this against master instead, either it would fail or, depending on exactly what I'm connected to, I could end up creating the rule in the wrong place entirely. That's the opposite of a server-level rule, which is created with sp_set_firewall_rule and specifically has to be run against master, since it applies at the server level rather than living inside one database. I always double-check my connection's current database in the query window before running either one, because this is an easy mix-up to make and the two procedures look almost identical in syntax.

Confusing sp_set_database_firewall_rule (database-level) with sp_set_firewall_rule (server-level, run against master)
Forgetting to verify the rule was created correctly by querying sys.database_firewall_rules
Specifying an IP range broader than actually needed instead of the narrowest range that satisfies the requirement

It must be executed while connected to that specific target database, not master
sys.database_firewall_rules can be queried to confirm the rule exists
This differs from the server-level sp_set_firewall_rule, which runs against master

questions.title: Writing the sys.dm_db_missing_index_details Diagnostic Query
questions.prompt: Write a query against the missing-index DMVs that returns the top 10 missing index suggestions for the current database, ranked by estimated overall impact (impact times how often SQL Server would have used it).
questions.modelAnswer: This requires joining three related DMVs: sys.dm_db_missing_index_details for the column details, sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups as the bridge table connecting a missing index handle to a group handle, and sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats for the usage and impact statistics. A reasonable overall-impact ranking multiplies avg_user_impact (the estimated percentage improvement) by (user_seeks + user_scans) (how many times the optimizer would have used it), then sorts descending and takes the top 10 with TOP (10).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd join the three DMVs in sequence: details for what columns are needed, groups as the join bridge between a missing-index handle and its stats, and group_stats for the actual numbers. For ranking, I don't just sort by avg_user_impact alone, because a huge estimated impact on a query that would only run twice a day doesn't matter as much as a modest impact on something that runs constantly -- so I multiply avg_user_impact by the combined seek and scan counts to get a rough 'total estimated benefit' number, and sort by that descending with TOP (10). I'd caveat this result the same way I always do with missing-index DMVs: it's a prioritized list of hypotheses to investigate against existing indexes and write-cost, not something to apply as-is without a second look.
questions.example:
SELECT TOP (10)
    mid.statement AS TableName,
    mid.equality_columns,
    mid.inequality_columns,
    mid.included_columns,
    migs.avg_user_impact,
    migs.user_seeks,
    migs.user_scans,
    migs.avg_user_impact * (migs.user_seeks + migs.user_scans) AS EstimatedOverallImpact
FROM sys.dm_db_missing_index_details mid
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups mig
    ON mid.index_handle = mig.index_handle
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats migs
    ON mig.index_group_handle = migs.group_handle
WHERE mid.database_id = DB_ID()
ORDER BY EstimatedOverallImpact DESC;
commonMistakes: Sorting only by avg_user_impact without factoring in how often the pattern actually occurs
Forgetting to join all three DMVs correctly (details to groups to group_stats)
Not filtering by database_id = DB_ID(), returning suggestions for other databases on the same instance
Treating the query's output as a direct action list without weighing existing indexes first
keyPoints: Three DMVs join together: missing_index_details, missing_index_groups, missing_index_group_stats
A combined impact-times-frequency metric ranks suggestions more meaningfully than impact alone
Filtering by database_id = DB_ID() scopes results to the current database
The result is a prioritized hypothesis list, not a direct action list

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly joins all three required DMVs
Correctly computes a combined impact-times-frequency ranking metric
Correctly scopes to the current database and limits to top 10
Query is syntactically valid T-SQL
