questions.title: Creating a SQL Agent Job With Two Steps in T-SQL
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL (using msdb system stored procedures) to create a SQL Agent job named 'Nightly Index Maintenance' with two steps -- rebuilding fragmented indexes, then updating statistics -- scheduled to run nightly at 1 AM.
questions.modelAnswer: Creating a job through T-SQL rather than the SSMS wizard means calling four msdb stored procedures in sequence: sp_add_job to create the job shell, sp_add_jobstep (called twice, once per step, each with an explicit on_success_action so the job flows from step 1 into step 2), sp_add_schedule to define the nightly 1 AM recurrence, sp_attach_schedule to attach that schedule to the job, and finally sp_add_jobserver to actually target the job at the local server (a job exists but won't run anywhere until it's attached to a server). Each jobstep's step_id must be assigned explicitly and in order, and the first step needs on_success_action = 3 (meaning 'go to next step') rather than the default of simply stopping after one step succeeds.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always build these in the same order, because missing one piece leaves the job half-configured and silently non-functional. First, sp_add_job creates the job itself as a named shell with no steps yet. Then sp_add_jobstep, called once per step with an explicit step_id, and critically, on the first step I set on_success_action = 3 so it proceeds to step 2 instead of just stopping -- that's the detail people forget, and the job then only ever runs its first step. After the steps, sp_add_schedule defines the actual recurrence -- nightly, 1 AM -- and sp_attach_schedule links that schedule to the job by name. The step people most often skip entirely is sp_add_jobserver -- without it, the job and schedule both exist in msdb, look completely normal in SSMS, but the job has no server to actually run on, so it just silently never fires. I always verify with a quick check against msdb.dbo.sysjobs and msdb.dbo.sysjobservers afterward to confirm it's genuinely wired up end to end.
commonMistakes: Forgetting sp_add_jobserver, leaving a job and schedule that exist but never actually run anywhere
Leaving the first step's on_success_action at its default, causing the job to stop instead of proceeding to step 2
Not assigning explicit, sequential step_id values when adding multiple steps
Confusing @freq_type and @freq_interval values, producing a schedule that doesn't actually run nightly
keyPoints: sp_add_job, sp_add_jobstep, sp_add_schedule, sp_attach_schedule, and sp_add_jobserver are all required
on_success_action = 3 on a step makes the job proceed to the next step instead of stopping
sp_add_jobserver is the step most often forgotten, leaving the job unable to actually run
Verifying against msdb.dbo.sysjobs and sysjobservers confirms the job is fully wired up

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly creates the job and both steps with sp_add_job/sp_add_jobstep
Correctly chains the steps with on_success_action
Correctly creates and attaches a nightly 1 AM schedule
Includes sp_add_jobserver so the job actually runs

questions.title: Finding the Head Blocker With DMVs
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query using sys.dm_exec_requests and sys.dm_exec_sessions that finds every session currently blocked, who is blocking it, and the blocking session's last run batch text. Explain how you'd use the result to find the head blocker in a chain of three or more sessions.
questions.modelAnswer: sys.dm_exec_requests has a blocking_session_id column that is non-zero exactly when a request is waiting on another session's lock, so filtering WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0 isolates every currently blocked request in one pass. Joining that back to sys.dm_exec_requests a second time (or to sys.dm_exec_sessions) on session_id = blocking_session_id pulls back what the blocker itself is running, and cross-applying sys.dm_exec_sql_text(sql_handle) turns the blocker's sql_handle into readable batch text. To find the head blocker in a chain of three or more -- A blocked by B, B blocked by C -- you walk the blocking_session_id column repeatedly: any session that appears as a blocking_session_id but whose own blocking_session_id is 0 (or NULL) is not waiting on anyone itself, which makes it the head blocker holding the lock everyone else is ultimately queued behind. Killing or waiting out that one session, not the ones in the middle of the chain, is what actually resolves the whole pileup.
questions.professionalAnswer: My starting query is always the same: pull sys.dm_exec_requests, filter blocking_session_id <> 0, and join it back to itself on session_id = blocking_session_id so I can see the blocker's own request sitting right next to the blocked one. I use sys.dm_exec_sql_text with CROSS APPLY to turn the blocker's sql_handle into actual readable SQL, because 'session 62 is blocking' tells me nothing -- I need to see what session 62 is actually running. The part people miss under pressure is that the session blocking you isn't always the real problem. If I see a chain -- session 80 blocked by 62, and 62 itself blocked by 55 -- the one query I actually need to kill or investigate is 55, because it's the one whose blocking_session_id is 0 or NULL, meaning nothing is holding it up. Everyone downstream of 55 just clears automatically the moment that root session commits or rolls back, so chasing session 62 would be wasted effort.
questions.example:
SELECT
    r.session_id            AS BlockedSessionID,
    r.blocking_session_id   AS BlockingSessionID,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    br.status                AS BlockerStatus,
    bt.text                  AS BlockerLastBatch
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
LEFT JOIN sys.dm_exec_requests AS br
    ON r.blocking_session_id = br.session_id
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(br.sql_handle) AS bt
WHERE r.blocking_session_id <> 0;
-- A session that never appears with a nonzero blocking_session_id of its own
-- is the head blocker: everything downstream is waiting, directly or
-- indirectly, on that one session.
commonMistakes: Killing the session that appears directly in blocking_session_id without checking whether that session is itself blocked by something further up the chain
Forgetting blocking_session_id is 0 (not NULL) for a request that isn't waiting on anyone
Not using CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text to see what the blocker is actually running, and guessing instead
Assuming the DMV snapshot represents a static picture, when blocking chains can shift between two queries run seconds apart
keyPoints: sys.dm_exec_requests.blocking_session_id identifies who is holding up a given request
Self-joining the DMV surfaces what the blocking session is actually running
The head blocker is the session whose own blocking_session_id is 0, with no one above it
Resolving the head blocker clears the whole downstream chain automatically

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly filters sys.dm_exec_requests for blocked sessions
Correctly joins to retrieve the blocking session's own activity
Correctly explains how to identify the head blocker in a multi-session chain
Provides valid, relevant example SQL

questions.title: Rebuild or Reorganize? Scripting the Decision
questions.prompt: Write T-SQL that queries sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats and decides, per index, whether to REORGANIZE, REBUILD, or do nothing, using the standard fragmentation thresholds. Explain why a maintenance job that always rebuilds every index regardless of fragmentation is a bad default.
questions.code:
-- avg_fragmentation_in_percent thresholds:
-- < 5%    : do nothing
-- 5-30%   : REORGANIZE
-- > 30%   : REBUILD
questions.modelAnswer: sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats returns avg_fragmentation_in_percent per index, and the long-standing Microsoft-recommended thresholds split the response into three bands: below roughly 5% fragmentation isn't worth touching at all, between 5% and 30% calls for REORGANIZE (an online, lighter-weight defragmentation of the existing leaf level), and above 30% calls for REBUILD (which drops and recreates the index, fully resolving fragmentation but at a much higher resource cost and, outside Enterprise Edition's ONLINE option, with a blocking schema modification lock). A script implements this by querying the DMV with a LIMITED or SAMPLED scan mode for routine jobs (DETAILED is far more expensive and usually reserved for investigation), then branching per index into REORGANIZE INDEX or ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD based on which band it falls in. Always rebuilding every index regardless of fragmentation is a bad default because REBUILD is expensive: it fully logs the operation (large in the full/bulk-logged recovery model), can briefly lock the table, and churns the buffer pool and transaction log for indexes that didn't actually need the work, every single maintenance window, whether or not fragmentation ever reached a level that would affect query performance.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always build this as a two-step process rather than a single hardcoded script: first, pull live fragmentation numbers from sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats using LIMITED or SAMPLED mode -- DETAILED actually scans every page and is far too expensive to run against every index in a production database on a schedule. Then I branch on the number I get back: under about 5%, I skip it entirely, because defragmenting an index that isn't fragmented just burns I/O and log space for nothing. Between 5% and 30%, REORGANIZE is enough -- it's always online, it just shuffles pages around at the leaf level without fully rebuilding the structure. Above 30%, I go to REBUILD, because reorganize alone won't meaningfully fix fragmentation that severe. The reason I push back hard on 'just rebuild everything every night' as a default is that rebuilding is genuinely expensive -- it's fully logged, it invalidates the plan cache for anything referencing that index, and on Standard Edition it takes a blocking lock for the duration. Doing that to a 50-million-row table that's sitting at 2% fragmentation is pure waste, every night, for no benefit.
questions.example:
DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) = N'';
SELECT @sql += CASE
    WHEN ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent > 30
        THEN 'ALTER INDEX ' + QUOTENAME(i.name) + ' ON ' + QUOTENAME(s.name) + '.' + QUOTENAME(t.name) + ' REBUILD;' + CHAR(10)
    WHEN ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent > 5
        THEN 'ALTER INDEX ' + QUOTENAME(i.name) + ' ON ' + QUOTENAME(s.name) + '.' + QUOTENAME(t.name) + ' REORGANIZE;' + CHAR(10)
    ELSE ''
END
FROM sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(DB_ID(), NULL, NULL, NULL, 'LIMITED') AS ips
JOIN sys.indexes AS i ON ips.object_id = i.object_id AND ips.index_id = i.index_id
JOIN sys.tables AS t ON i.object_id = t.object_id
JOIN sys.schemas AS s ON t.schema_id = s.schema_id
WHERE ips.index_id > 0 AND ips.page_count > 1000;
EXEC sp_executesql @sql;
commonMistakes: Running sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats in DETAILED mode across every database as a routine nightly job, adding unnecessary I/O load
Rebuilding every index regardless of fragmentation level, rather than branching by threshold
Forgetting that REBUILD takes a blocking schema modification lock outside the Enterprise Edition ONLINE option
Skipping the page_count filter, which wastes effort defragmenting tiny indexes where fragmentation is cosmetic
keyPoints: sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats exposes avg_fragmentation_in_percent per index
Standard thresholds: under 5% skip, 5-30% REORGANIZE, over 30% REBUILD
REBUILD is far more expensive than REORGANIZE and shouldn't be the default for every index
LIMITED/SAMPLED scan modes are appropriate for routine jobs; DETAILED is for investigation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and applies the standard fragmentation thresholds
Correctly distinguishes REORGANIZE from REBUILD in cost and behavior
Explains why always-rebuild is a bad default
Provides valid, relevant example SQL

questions.title: Reading a Plan's Missing Index Warning
questions.prompt: You run a query in SSMS with 'Include Actual Execution Plan' on, and the plan shows a green, dashed 'Missing Index' suggestion with an impact score. Walk through exactly what you'd check before creating that index, and what in the plan itself would tell you the table is being scanned instead of seeked.
questions.modelAnswer: The green dashed missing-index box in a graphical plan is SQL Server's optimizer reporting, for this one specific query, which equality columns, inequality columns, and included columns would have let it use an index it didn't have -- the impact percentage is the optimizer's own rough estimate of relative improvement, not a guarantee. Before creating it, you'd check the base operator the plan actually used: a Table Scan or an Index Scan on a large row count (visible by hovering the operator for 'Estimated Number of Rows' or 'Actual Number of Rows') confirms SQL Server read far more of the table than the query logically needed, which is exactly the situation a well-chosen index fixes by letting the optimizer switch to an Index Seek instead -- a seek navigates directly to matching rows via the B-tree rather than reading every page. You'd also check whether an existing index already covers most of the same columns, since the missing-index feature has no awareness of what's already there and will suggest a near-duplicate of something that already exists. Finally, you'd weigh the suggestion against how often this exact query pattern actually runs and the table's write volume, since every new index adds maintenance overhead to every insert, update, and delete against that table going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I see that green dashed missing-index box, the first thing I do is right-click the base table operator itself and compare 'Estimated Number of Rows' against what a seek on a good index would actually need to touch -- if it's a Table Scan or an unselective Index Scan pulling back hundreds of thousands of rows for a query that logically needs a handful, that confirms the plan really is doing unnecessary work, not just that the optimizer is being hopeful. Then I go check sys.indexes on that table before I create anything, because the missing-index suggestion has zero awareness of what already exists -- I've seen it recommend an index that's 90% identical to one already sitting there, just with columns in a slightly different order. If nothing overlaps and the scan is genuinely large, I'll create the suggested index, but I always reorder the equality columns the way the query actually filters and add the included columns explicitly rather than copy-pasting the DMV's suggestion verbatim, since the suggestion's column ordering isn't always the one that produces the tightest seek.
commonMistakes: Creating the exact suggested index without checking whether a near-duplicate already exists on the table
Treating the impact percentage as a guaranteed performance gain rather than a rough optimizer estimate
Not checking the actual operator (Scan vs. Seek) and row counts before deciding the suggestion is worth acting on
Ignoring the write-cost tradeoff of adding a new index to a heavily-written table
keyPoints: The missing-index suggestion lists equality, inequality, and included columns for this specific query
A Scan operator with a large row count is the visual confirmation that an index would help
The suggestion has no awareness of existing indexes and can recommend a near-duplicate
A new index should be weighed against its write-maintenance cost, not created automatically

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what the missing-index suggestion represents
Correctly identifies Scan vs. Seek as the visual signal in the plan
Correctly describes checking for existing index overlap before creating one
Mentions the write-cost tradeoff of adding the index

questions.title: Checking Backup Health Across a Server With dbatools
questions.prompt: Write a PowerShell snippet using dbatools that connects to a SQL Server instance and reports every database whose last full backup is older than 24 hours. Explain why you'd use Get-DbaLastBackup instead of querying msdb.dbo.backupset directly in a reusable script.
questions.modelAnswer: Get-DbaLastBackup is a dbatools cmdlet that, for every database on a target instance, returns the last full, differential, and log backup dates along with calculated fields like database size and days-since-backup, having already handled the underlying msdb.dbo.backupset/backupmediafamily joins, filtering out TDE-certificate-only entries, and accounting for databases with no backup history at all. Piping its output through Where-Object on the LastFullBackup property compared against (Get-Date).AddHours(-24) isolates exactly the databases overdue for a backup. The reason to prefer the cmdlet over hand-rolling the msdb query every time: msdb's backup tables have real subtleties (a database can show up multiple times for a striped backup across several backup_set rows, mirrored backups complicate the join further, and model/tempdb need special-casing) that dbatools has already solved, tested, and maintained across SQL Server versions -- writing and maintaining that T-SQL yourself in every automation script is reinventing something the community has already gotten right, and more fragile to SQL Server version differences.
questions.professionalAnswer: My go-to one-liner for this is Get-DbaLastBackup against the instance, piped into a filter on LastFullBackup older than 24 hours -- it's maybe three lines of PowerShell and I get back a clean object I can pipe into Export-Csv, Send-MailMessage, or straight into a Teams webhook. The reason I don't just hand-write the msdb query instead, even though I know how, is that msdb.dbo.backupset is genuinely trickier than it looks the moment you have striped backups across multiple files, or a database that's never been backed up at all and simply has no rows -- dbatools has already handled those edge cases and tested them across SQL Server versions, so I'm not maintaining my own brittle version of the same logic in every script I write. I only drop down to raw T-SQL against msdb myself when I need something dbatools genuinely doesn't expose, which is rare for a basic backup-health check like this one.
questions.example:
Import-Module dbatools

$cutoff = (Get-Date).AddHours(-24)

Get-DbaLastBackup -SqlInstance 'SQLPROD01' |
    Where-Object { $_.LastFullBackup -lt $cutoff -or $null -eq $_.LastFullBackup } |
    Select-Object Database, LastFullBackup, LastDiffBackup, LastLogBackup |
    Format-Table -AutoSize
commonMistakes: Hand-writing a fresh msdb.dbo.backupset query in every script instead of using the maintained dbatools cmdlet
Forgetting that a database with no backup history returns null rather than a date, and not handling that case in the filter
Not accounting for system databases (model, tempdb) that have different backup expectations
Comparing against the wrong backup type (checking LastDiffBackup when the requirement is specifically about full backups)
keyPoints: Get-DbaLastBackup returns last full/diff/log backup dates per database in one call
It already handles msdb join subtleties like striped and mirrored backups
Filtering on LastFullBackup against a time cutoff isolates overdue databases
Reusing a maintained cmdlet is more reliable than re-deriving the same logic from msdb repeatedly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses Get-DbaLastBackup with an appropriate filter
Correctly explains the msdb join subtleties dbatools abstracts away
Provides valid, runnable PowerShell
Handles or mentions the no-backup-history edge case

questions.title: Creating a Matching User Across Three Platforms
questions.prompt: You need to create a read-only reporting user named rpt_reader that can SELECT from one schema, on SQL Server, Oracle, and PostgreSQL. Write the equivalent commands for each platform and point out the one conceptual difference that trips up SQL Server DBAs moving to Oracle for the first time.
questions.modelAnswer: On SQL Server, creating access is a two-step, two-object process: CREATE LOGIN at the server level establishes who can connect, and CREATE USER inside the target database, mapped to that login, establishes what they can access there -- then GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::ReportingSchema grants the read access. PostgreSQL is conceptually similar to SQL Server's model: CREATE ROLE rpt_reader LOGIN PASSWORD '...' creates a connectable role, and GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA reporting TO rpt_reader plus GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA reporting TO rpt_reader grants the actual access, with USAGE being the easy-to-forget step since without it SELECT alone still can't even see into the schema. Oracle is where the conceptual model actually changes: CREATE USER rpt_reader IDENTIFIED BY ... creates a schema-owning account in the same step as creating the login-equivalent -- in Oracle, a user and a schema are effectively the same thing, so there's no separate server-login-to-database-user mapping step the way SQL Server and PostgreSQL both have. The specific trip-up for SQL Server DBAs moving to Oracle: in SQL Server, a login and a database user are deliberately two separate objects precisely so one login can map to users in multiple databases, but Oracle collapses that distinction -- creating an Oracle user always creates (or is identical to) a schema, which feels wrong the first time to anyone used to SQL Server's two-layer security model.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through these in the order people usually learn them. SQL Server: CREATE LOGIN at the instance level, then CREATE USER inside the database mapped to that login, then GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::ReportingSchema TO rpt_reader -- that's the two-object model most DBAs already know cold. PostgreSQL maps onto that almost one-for-one: CREATE ROLE rpt_reader LOGIN PASSWORD '...', then GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA reporting TO rpt_reader before GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA reporting TO rpt_reader -- the one thing I always flag for people new to Postgres is that USAGE grant; forgetting it is probably the single most common 'why can't my user see anything' ticket in Postgres. Oracle is the one that genuinely surprises SQL Server people: CREATE USER rpt_reader IDENTIFIED BY '...' doesn't just create a login-equivalent, it creates a schema with that exact name, because in Oracle a user IS a schema -- there's no separate mapping step. The mental model shift I always explain up front is: stop thinking 'login maps to a user in a database' the SQL Server way, and start thinking 'this account owns its own schema' the Oracle way -- it's a genuinely different architecture, not just different syntax for the same idea.
commonMistakes: Forgetting PostgreSQL's GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA step, leaving the user unable to see anything despite having SELECT
Assuming Oracle has a separate login-to-user mapping step the way SQL Server and PostgreSQL do
Forgetting Oracle requires GRANT CREATE SESSION before the user can even connect

Assuming GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA in PostgreSQL retroactively covers tables created after the grant, when it only covers tables existing at grant time unless paired with ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES
keyPoints: SQL Server and PostgreSQL both separate a connectable login/role from schema-level access grants
PostgreSQL requires an explicit USAGE grant on the schema before SELECT grants are useful
Oracle collapses user and schema into a single concept with no separate mapping step
This is a genuine architectural difference, not just syntax, and it's the main adjustment for SQL Server DBAs learning Oracle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Provides correct, working SQL Server user-creation and grant syntax
Provides correct, working PostgreSQL role-creation and grant syntax, including USAGE
Provides correct, working Oracle user-creation and grant syntax
Correctly explains the user-equals-schema conceptual difference in Oracle

questions.title: Diagnosing a deadlock between two ETL jobs
questions.prompt: Two nightly stored procedures occasionally fail with a deadlock error when they run at overlapping times, each updating the same two tables. Explain what a deadlock is, how SQL Server resolves it automatically, and two concrete things you'd change to prevent it from recurring.
questions.modelAnswer: Blocking happens whenever one transaction needs a lock another transaction already holds, and simply waits -- this is normal and expected. A deadlock is the special case where Transaction A is waiting on a lock held by Transaction B, while B is simultaneously waiting on a lock held by A -- neither can ever proceed. SQL Server detects this automatically and picks one transaction as the 'deadlock victim,' rolling it back and raising an error, while the other transaction proceeds normally. To prevent recurrence: (1) access the two tables in the same order in both procedures -- a common deadlock cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; and (2) keep transactions as short as possible, doing only what genuinely needs to be atomic inside BEGIN/COMMIT, so locks are held for the shortest possible window and the overlap that triggers the deadlock has a smaller chance of occurring.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by reassuring whoever's asking that blocking itself isn't a bug -- it's how isolation is enforced any time two transactions genuinely need the same data at the same moment. A deadlock is the specific, more serious case: A is waiting on a lock B holds, B is waiting on a lock A holds, and neither can ever win -- it's a true standoff. SQL Server doesn't just hang forever; it detects the cycle and picks a 'deadlock victim' to roll back automatically, which is why the application sees an error and needs to retry. For the actual fix, the first thing I'd check is whether both procedures touch the two tables in a different order -- that's the single most common cause, and standardizing the access order so both procedures always touch, say, Table A before Table B usually eliminates it outright. Second, I'd look at whether either transaction is doing more than it needs to inside BEGIN/COMMIT -- unrelated reads, validation logic -- and trim the transaction down to just the atomic part, since shorter transactions hold locks for less time and collide less often.
commonMistakes: Treating a deadlock the same as ordinary blocking -- blocking is normal, a deadlock is a genuine, unresolvable standoff
Assuming SQL Server will just hang forever instead of recognizing it auto-detects and resolves deadlocks
Fixing the symptom by adding a retry loop in the application without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Making a transaction longer by adding error handling or logging inside it, which increases lock duration
keyPoints: Blocking is normal; a deadlock is two transactions waiting on each other with no way out
SQL Server auto-detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen 'victim' transaction
The victim's application should retry the transaction
Accessing tables in a consistent order across procedures prevents most deadlocks
Shortening transactions reduces how long locks are held and how often collisions occur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes blocking from a deadlock
Correctly explains SQL Server's automatic deadlock resolution
Proposes consistent table access order as a concrete fix
Proposes shortening transactions as a concrete fix

questions.title: A query got slow after it used to be fast
questions.prompt: A report query that filters WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 used to run instantly and now takes minutes as the table has grown. There is an index on OrderDate. Diagnose why the index isn't helping, and rewrite the WHERE clause so it is.
questions.modelAnswer: The predicate is non-SARGable: wrapping the OrderDate column in the YEAR() function forces SQL Server to compute YEAR(OrderDate) for every single row before it can compare against 2013, which means the index on the raw OrderDate column can't be used -- it stores actual dates, not year-extracted values. This was barely noticeable on a small table (a full scan of a few hundred rows is instant either way), but as the table grows into the millions of rows, the same non-SARGable predicate turns a sub-second query into one that takes minutes. The fix is to rewrite the condition so the column itself is left untouched, and transform the comparison value instead: WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2014-01-01'. This asks the identical logical question but lets SQL Server use the index on OrderDate to jump directly to the matching range.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a textbook SARGability problem, and the giveaway is right there in the WHERE clause -- there's a function wrapped around the column. Any time I see YEAR(SomeDateColumn), UPPER(SomeColumn), or similar, my first instinct is: the index on that raw column can't be used, because SQL Server would have to transform every row's value before it could compare it, and an index doesn't store transformed values. The reason it 'used to be fast' is simply table size -- a full scan is invisible on a small table and brutal on a large one, so this kind of bug often doesn't show up until data volume grows past some threshold. The fix is always the same shape: stop transforming the column, and transform the comparison value instead. Instead of asking 'what year is this date in,' I ask 'is this date within the 2013 calendar year range' -- same answer, but now the raw OrderDate column is untouched in the comparison, so the existing index can be used for a range scan instead of a full scan.
commonMistakes: Blaming the index itself ('the index must be corrupt/fragmented') instead of the predicate wrapping the column
Rewriting to BETWEEN '2013-01-01' AND '2013-12-31' and accidentally excluding rows with a time component on Dec 31
Not recognizing other common non-SARGable patterns like UPPER(column) = 'X' or a leading-wildcard LIKE '%text'
Assuming the problem only appears with YEAR() and missing that any function on the column causes the same issue
keyPoints: SARGable means the predicate can use an index directly; non-SARGable forces a full scan
Wrapping the column in a function (YEAR, UPPER, etc.) makes a predicate non-SARGable
Fix by transforming the comparison value instead of the column
The performance gap only becomes visible as table size grows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the predicate as non-SARGable and explains why
Correctly explains why this matters more as the table grows
Provides a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite
Rewrite correctly handles the full year's date range without off-by-one errors

questions.title: A report is hanging, but there's no deadlock error
questions.prompt: Users report that a dashboard query has been 'just spinning' for several minutes, but no deadlock error ever appears. Explain the difference between this situation and a deadlock, how you'd identify the actual head blocker, and what you'd check before deciding to kill the blocking session.
questions.modelAnswer: This is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- a deadlock is a genuine standoff that SQL Server detects and resolves automatically within seconds by killing a victim; it never just hangs indefinitely. Plain blocking, by contrast, can hang as long as whatever is holding the lock keeps holding it, because there's no cycle for SQL Server to detect -- one session is simply waiting its turn behind another, and nothing resolves that automatically. To find the actual head blocker, I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests, specifically looking at the blocking_session_id column -- the session with a non-zero blocking_session_id is being blocked, and the session that ID points to (which itself usually shows blocking_session_id = 0) is the head blocker actually holding the lock everyone's waiting on. Before killing that session, I'd check what it's actually doing -- its SQL text, and whether it's an open, uncommitted transaction (an application that opened a transaction and is sitting idle, or a long-running batch job that's legitimately mid-write). Killing a session mid-write rolls back whatever it was doing, which can be worse than the wait itself if it's a large, mostly-finished operation -- so I'd rather understand what it's doing and consider letting it finish or committing/rolling it back cleanly than reflexively kill it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd clarify, because it changes the whole response, is that this isn't a deadlock -- SQL Server resolves deadlocks on its own, usually within seconds, by picking a victim and rolling it back. If nothing has errored and the query is just sitting there, that's plain blocking: one session waiting on a lock another session is holding, with no cycle, so nothing forces a resolution automatically. My first query is always against sys.dm_exec_requests, looking at blocking_session_id -- that tells me directly who's blocked and, by following the chain, who the actual head blocker is, as opposed to the session that looks blocked but is itself only blocked by someone else further up. Once I've got the head blocker's session ID, I'd pull its actual SQL text and check whether it's sitting inside an open transaction that was never committed, versus genuinely mid-execution on a big write. That distinction decides what I do next -- if it's an application bug that opened a transaction and forgot to close it, killing the session is reasonable and I'd also flag that bug separately. If it's a legitimate long-running batch load that's 90% done, killing it rolls back all of that work and probably makes things worse, so I'd rather let it finish, or coordinate with whoever owns that job before touching it.
questions.example:
-- Find who's blocking whom
SELECT session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, status
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0;

-- Follow the chain to the head blocker (blocking_session_id = 0, but others point to it)
-- Then inspect what the head blocker is actually running:
SELECT text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.session_id = @HeadBlockerSessionId;
commonMistakes: Treating any hanging query as a deadlock, when a true deadlock is auto-resolved within seconds, not left hanging
Killing the first blocked session found instead of tracing blocking_session_id to the actual head blocker
Killing a session without checking whether it's mid-write on a legitimate long-running job
Not distinguishing an application bug (an abandoned open transaction) from a genuinely busy, legitimate session
keyPoints: A hanging query with no error is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- deadlocks auto-resolve quickly
sys.dm_exec_requests' blocking_session_id column traces the blocking chain to the actual head blocker
Check what the head blocker is actually doing before killing it -- an abandoned transaction vs. a legitimate long write
Killing a session mid-write rolls back its work, which can be worse than waiting for it to finish

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes ordinary blocking from a deadlock
Correctly identifies how to find the head blocker (sys.dm_exec_requests / blocking_session_id)
Explains what to check before killing the blocking session
Provides correct, relevant diagnostic SQL

questions.title: A Covering Index Isn't Helping, and Nobody Knows Why
questions.prompt: A table has a nonclustered index covering exactly the columns a report query needs, but the query's execution plan still shows a full scan instead of using the index. The query is SELECT * FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. What's the most likely cause, and how would you fix the query?
questions.modelAnswer: SELECT * is almost certainly the cause. A covering index only helps when the query asks for columns the index actually includes; SELECT * asks for every column in the table, regardless of what's actually needed, which defeats the index's coverage the moment even one requested column isn't part of it. SQL Server then has to fall back to either a Key Lookup for each matching row or a full scan, depending on cost, instead of satisfying the query entirely from the narrower index. The fix is to name only the columns the report genuinely needs instead of SELECT *: SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. If those four columns are exactly what the covering index includes, the optimizer can now satisfy the entire query from the index alone, without ever touching the underlying table.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before touching the index, I'd actually look at the execution plan and the exact columns requested, because 'should use the index but doesn't' almost always traces back to the SELECT list, not the index definition. SELECT * is the first thing I'd check, because it's such a common habit and such a direct cause: if the index only covers four specific columns and the query asks for all fifteen columns on the table via *, the index simply can't satisfy that request on its own, and SQL Server has to go fetch the rest from the table itself — either via a Key Lookup per row or by abandoning the index entirely for a full scan, depending on how many rows are involved. The fix is almost always just naming the specific columns the report actually displays instead of *. I'd also double check that the index's included columns genuinely match what the report needs, because if even one required column is missing from the index, the same fallback happens no matter how narrowly I write the SELECT list.
commonMistakes: Assuming the index itself must be broken or missing, without checking what columns the query actually requests
Rebuilding or recreating the index before checking the SELECT list, missing the actual cause
Not verifying the index's included columns genuinely cover everything the trimmed SELECT list needs
Fixing this one query but not checking other queries against the same table for the identical SELECT * habit
keyPoints: SELECT * requests every column, defeating a covering index that only includes some of them
The fallback is a Key Lookup per row, or a full scan, instead of satisfying the query from the index alone
The fix is naming exactly the columns actually needed
The index's included columns must still genuinely match what's requested for this fix to work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies SELECT * as the likely cause
Correctly explains why it defeats a covering index
Provides a correct fix naming specific columns
Notes the fix depends on the index already covering those exact columns

questions.title: A Reporting Tool Suddenly Can't Reach Azure SQL
questions.prompt: A reporting application that has connected to an Azure SQL database successfully for months suddenly starts failing with connection timeout errors. Nothing about the application code changed. Walk through how you'd narrow down whether this is a firewall, VNet, or a genuinely different problem.
questions.modelAnswer: The investigation should move from most-likely-and-cheapest-to-check toward more exotic causes. First, check whether the reporting application's outbound IP actually changed -- a cloud-hosted app behind a dynamic IP or a NAT gateway can change its egress IP without any application code changing at all, which would make a previously-allowed firewall rule now block it; comparing the app's current public IP against what's actually listed in the Azure SQL server's firewall rules settles this quickly. Second, check Azure SQL's own connectivity diagnostics and the Azure Monitor/connectivity logs for the server, which often show a specific blocked-connection-attempt entry naming the source IP that got rejected -- turning a guess into a confirmed fact. Third, if a VNet rule or Private Endpoint is involved rather than a plain IP firewall rule, check whether anything changed on the network side -- a route table, an NSG rule, a peering change -- since those can silently break connectivity with zero application-level change. Only after ruling out all three would it be reasonable to suspect something odd at the database engine level, like a resource-governor throttling event or the server being paused (for serverless tier).
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't touch application code at all first, since nothing there changed -- I'd start with the cheapest, most likely external cause: has the app's outbound IP changed? That happens more than people expect, especially behind a NAT gateway, a load balancer, or a cloud provider that doesn't guarantee a static egress IP, and it would make a previously-fine firewall rule start rejecting connections with zero code change on either side. I'd check the app's current public IP against exactly what's listed on the Azure SQL server's firewall rules to confirm or rule that out directly. If that's not it, I'd go look at Azure SQL's connectivity diagnostics, which often log the actual rejected connection attempt with the source IP -- that turns this from a guess into a fact I can act on. If this environment uses a VNet rule or Private Endpoint instead of a plain IP allowlist, I'd widen the search to the network side -- has an NSG rule, route table, or peering configuration changed recently, since none of those require an app code change to break connectivity. Only once I've ruled out all of that would I start looking at anything unusual on the database side itself, like whether this is a serverless tier database that auto-paused.
commonMistakes: Assuming the application code must be the cause when it genuinely hasn't changed, ignoring external network factors
Not checking whether the application's outbound IP changed, which is a very common silent cause
Skipping Azure SQL's connectivity diagnostics/logs, which often name the exact rejected connection attempt
Jumping straight to an exotic database-engine explanation before ruling out the simpler network-level causes
keyPoints: Check whether the app's outbound IP changed, which can silently break a previously-working firewall rule
Azure SQL connectivity diagnostics/logs often show the specific rejected connection attempt
If a VNet rule or Private Endpoint is in play, check for NSG, route table, or peering changes
Investigation should move from cheapest/most-likely causes to more exotic ones, not the reverse

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Checks for a changed outbound IP as a likely first cause
Uses Azure SQL connectivity diagnostics/logs to confirm rather than guess
Considers VNet/NSG/Private Endpoint changes as a distinct possible cause
Investigates in a logical order from likely to exotic causes

questions.title: A SQL Agent Job Shows Success, But the Work Didn't Happen
questions.prompt: A nightly SQL Agent job that runs an index maintenance stored procedure has shown 'Succeeded' every night for two weeks, but index fragmentation has been climbing the whole time as if the job never actually ran. What would you check, and what's the most likely explanation?
questions.modelAnswer: A job step reporting 'Succeeded' only means the T-SQL batch it ran completed without raising an error -- it says nothing about whether that batch actually did meaningful work. The most likely explanation is that the stored procedure itself is silently doing less than expected: a WHERE clause or a fragmentation threshold check inside the procedure that's evaluating false for every table (for example, checking against the wrong database context, or a threshold that's never actually met due to a logic bug), causing the procedure to run, find nothing matching its criteria, and exit cleanly -- which SQL Agent correctly reports as success, because no error occurred. The first thing to check is the job step's actual output/history details (not just the green checkmark) for row counts or a log the procedure might write; the second is running the stored procedure manually and watching exactly what it does, with PRINT statements or a debugger, to see whether it's iterating over any tables at all. A less likely but worth-checking possibility is the job running against the wrong database context if the step doesn't explicitly specify one.
questions.professionalAnswer: The green checkmark is the first thing I'd stop trusting here, because 'Succeeded' from SQL Agent only means the batch didn't throw an error -- it doesn't mean the batch did anything useful. My bet, before even looking, is that the stored procedure's own logic is silently finding nothing to do every single night -- maybe a fragmentation threshold check that's comparing against the wrong column or using an operator that's always false, so the procedure runs, loops over zero tables, and exits cleanly, which is a perfectly valid 'success' from SQL Agent's point of view. I'd go check the job step's history output directly, not just the pass/fail icon, to see if it logs anything like a row count or table count that would immediately show 'processed 0 tables.' If the procedure doesn't log anything useful itself, I'd just run it manually in SSMS and add some quick PRINT statements to see exactly what it's iterating over and why it's apparently skipping everything. I'd also double-check the job step is actually running in the context of the right database -- a step with no explicit USE statement running against the wrong default database is a classic, easy-to-miss cause of exactly this symptom.
commonMistakes: Trusting the 'Succeeded' status as proof the procedure did meaningful work, rather than just that it didn't error
Not checking the job step's detailed history/output for row counts or logged information
Assuming the job scheduling itself is broken rather than suspecting the procedure's own internal logic
Forgetting to check whether the step is running against the intended database context
keyPoints: A 'Succeeded' job status means no error occurred, not that meaningful work happened
A silent logic bug inside the procedure (a threshold or condition that's never true) can cause it to do nothing and still succeed
Checking job step history output/logs for actual row/table counts reveals the real activity
Running the procedure manually with diagnostic output is the fastest way to see what it's actually doing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that 'Succeeded' only means no error, not that work occurred
Proposes checking job step history/output for actual activity evidence
Proposes running the procedure manually to diagnose the silent logic issue
Mentions checking the database execution context as a possible cause

lessonLink.label: Review: Troubleshooting Failed SQL Agent Jobs

questions.title: Query Store Shows a Plan Regression Right After a Deployment
questions.prompt: Users report a report page got noticeably slower the same day a new application release went out. Query Store shows the underlying query now has two distinct plans, and the newer one has much higher average duration. Walk through what you'd do.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a textbook plan regression, and Query Store's specific value here is that it retains both the old, better-performing plan and the new, worse one side by side, instead of only showing whatever is currently cached. The first step is confirming the regression with actual numbers -- comparing average duration, logical reads, and CPU between the two plan IDs in the Query Store reports, to verify this isn't a coincidence but a genuine, measurable regression tied to the deployment date. If the old plan is confirmed better and the underlying query/schema hasn't changed in a way that invalidates it, Query Store allows forcing that previous plan back on immediately through sp_query_store_force_plan, which restores acceptable performance right away as a mitigation. In parallel, the actual root cause still needs investigating -- a deployment can trigger a plan regression through a statistics update, a parameter-sensitive query getting compiled with an atypically-shaped first parameter (parameter sniffing), or a schema/index change bundled into the same release -- and that root cause, not just the forced plan, is what needs a permanent fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: The timing lines up too well to be a coincidence, so I'd treat this as a plan regression from the start and let Query Store do what it's actually built for. First I'd pull up both plan IDs for this query in Query Store and look at the actual numbers side by side -- duration, reads, CPU -- to confirm the new plan really is worse and by how much, rather than going on a vague user complaint alone. If it's confirmed and the old plan is still valid for the query as it exists today, I'd force the old plan back on with sp_query_store_force_plan immediately -- that's a fast, safe mitigation that gets users back to acceptable performance right now, while I keep investigating. The investigation itself is about why the plan changed at exactly that moment -- did the deployment touch an index, did it coincide with a statistics update, or is this parameter sniffing, where the query got recompiled and happened to compile against an atypical parameter value right around deployment time. I wouldn't consider this done just because the forced plan fixed the symptom -- I'd want the actual cause understood so I'm not just going to keep manually re-forcing a plan every time this happens again.
questions.example:
-- Compare plan performance for the same query
SELECT qsp.plan_id, qsrs.avg_duration, qsrs.avg_cpu_time, qsrs.avg_logical_io_reads, qsrs.count_executions
FROM sys.query_store_plan qsp
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats qsrs ON qsp.plan_id = qsrs.plan_id
WHERE qsp.query_id = @QueryId
ORDER BY qsrs.avg_duration DESC;

-- Force the previous, better-performing plan back on as an immediate mitigation
EXEC sp_query_store_force_plan @query_id = @QueryId, @plan_id = @GoodPlanId;
commonMistakes: Fixing only by forcing the old plan without ever investigating why the regression actually happened
Assuming a plan regression always means a code bug, rather than considering statistics updates or parameter sniffing
Not confirming the regression with actual Query Store numbers before acting, relying only on anecdotal reports
Forgetting that a forced plan should be revisited later -- it's a mitigation, not necessarily a permanent fix if the query or schema changes again
keyPoints: Query Store retains multiple historical plans, making a regression comparison possible
Confirming the regression with actual duration/CPU/reads numbers avoids acting on assumption
sp_query_store_force_plan can restore the previous plan as an immediate mitigation
The root cause (statistics, parameter sniffing, schema/index change) still needs investigating separately

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies this as a plan regression and confirms it with Query Store data
Correctly proposes forcing the previous plan as an immediate mitigation
Investigates the actual root cause rather than stopping at the mitigation
Provides correct, relevant Query Store SQL

lessonLink.label: Review: Using Query Store to Find Regressed Queries

questions.title: A Query Is Slow, But There's No Blocking and No Missing Index
questions.prompt: A specific stored procedure is consistently slow, but there's no blocking session, and the execution plan shows it's using all the expected indexes. Which DMVs would you check next to figure out what the query is actually waiting on?
questions.modelAnswer: With blocking and missing indexes both ruled out, the next step is looking at wait statistics, because 'slow' almost always means the query is spending time waiting on something specific, even without another session blocking it. sys.dm_exec_requests (while the query is actually running) shows the current wait_type and wait_time for the live session, which names exactly what it's waiting on right now -- common candidates include PAGEIOLATCH waits (waiting on physical disk I/O to read data pages), CXPACKET/CXCONSUMER (parallelism coordination overhead), or RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE (waiting for memory grant). For a pattern across multiple past executions rather than one live snapshot, sys.dm_exec_query_stats combined with sys.dm_exec_sql_text gives aggregate statistics (total/average worker time, logical reads, elapsed time) per query, which can reveal whether the time is mostly CPU-bound (high worker_time relative to elapsed_time) or I/O-bound (high logical/physical reads). The specific wait type found points to a specific next step -- PAGEIOLATCH points toward I/O subsystem or buffer pool pressure, RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE points toward memory grant sizing, and so on.
questions.professionalAnswer: If blocking and missing indexes are both ruled out, my next move is always wait statistics, because the query has to be spending its time somewhere, and the wait type names exactly where. While it's actually running, sys.dm_exec_requests shows the live wait_type and wait_time for that session -- that's the fastest way to catch it in the act. If I can't catch it live, or I want to see a pattern across many executions rather than one snapshot, I'd go to sys.dm_exec_query_stats joined to sys.dm_exec_sql_text, which gives me aggregate numbers per query -- total worker time, total elapsed time, logical and physical reads -- and the relationship between those tells its own story: if worker_time is close to elapsed_time, it's mostly CPU-bound; if elapsed_time is much higher than worker_time with high physical reads, it's probably waiting on I/O. Whatever specific wait type shows up changes what I do next -- PAGEIOLATCH sends me looking at the storage layer or buffer pool pressure, RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE sends me looking at memory grants and possibly Resource Governor settings, CXPACKET sends me looking at parallelism (MAXDOP) settings. The wait type is the actual clue; I wouldn't guess at a fix before I have it.
questions.example:
-- Live wait info while the query is actually running
SELECT r.session_id, r.wait_type, r.wait_time, r.status, t.text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.session_id <> @@SPID;

-- Aggregate stats across past executions of the same query
SELECT qs.total_worker_time, qs.total_elapsed_time, qs.total_logical_reads,
       qs.execution_count, t.text
FROM sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) t
WHERE t.text LIKE '%YourProcedureName%';
commonMistakes: Stopping the investigation once blocking and missing indexes are ruled out, without checking wait statistics
Not distinguishing a CPU-bound pattern from an I/O-bound pattern using worker_time vs. elapsed_time
Assuming a specific wait type without actually querying the DMVs to confirm it
Jumping to a fix (adding hardware, rewriting the query) before identifying the actual wait type causing the delay
keyPoints: sys.dm_exec_requests shows the live wait_type/wait_time for a currently-running session
sys.dm_exec_query_stats combined with sys.dm_exec_sql_text shows aggregate behavior across past executions
Comparing worker_time to elapsed_time distinguishes CPU-bound from I/O-bound patterns
The specific wait type found should drive the next diagnostic step, not a guess

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes checking wait statistics given blocking/indexing are ruled out
Correctly uses sys.dm_exec_requests for live wait information
Correctly uses sys.dm_exec_query_stats for historical patterns
Connects a specific wait type to a sensible next diagnostic direction

lessonLink.label: Review: DMVs for Query Performance Troubleshooting

questions.title: A Failover Group Test Leaves the App Still Pointing at the Old Primary
questions.prompt: During a planned DR test, you fail over an Auto-Failover Group to the secondary region. The failover itself succeeds, but the application keeps writing to the old primary's connection string instead of automatically routing to the new primary. What went wrong, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is that the application was never actually configured to use the failover group's listener endpoint -- it's pointed at the specific server name of the original primary directly, bypassing the entire mechanism a failover group provides. The listener endpoint is a stable DNS name that always resolves to whichever database is currently primary; if the application's connection string hardcodes the original server's name instead, failing over the group changes which database is primary, but the application has no way to know that, because it never asked the listener -- it's still talking directly to the old primary, which is now a read-only secondary (writes would actually start failing, not silently succeed, which is the real giveaway here). The fix is updating the application's connection string to use the failover group's listener endpoint instead of a specific server name, and then re-running the DR test to confirm the application actually follows the failover automatically this time.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is almost always a connection-string problem, not a failover-group problem -- the failover group did its job; the application just never asked it the right question. The whole point of the listener endpoint is that it's a stable name that always points at whichever side is currently primary, so the application should never need to know or care which region that is. If the app's connection string has the original server's actual name hardcoded instead of the listener's name, failing over the group doesn't help it at all, because it's not going through the listener in the first place -- it's still talking directly to the old primary, which should now be read-only, so writes should actually be failing outright rather than silently landing somewhere wrong, which is worth double-checking too since that's the real symptom that confirms this diagnosis. The fix is updating the connection string to the failover group's listener endpoint and then genuinely re-running the DR test, not just assuming the fix worked, because the whole point of a DR test is catching exactly this kind of gap before a real outage does.
commonMistakes: Assuming the failover group itself malfunctioned rather than checking the application's actual connection string
Not recognizing that writes to the old primary should start failing (it's now read-only), not silently succeeding
Fixing the connection string but not re-running the DR test to actually confirm the fix works
Confusing the listener endpoint's DNS name with the original server's name, assuming they're interchangeable
keyPoints: A failover group's listener endpoint is what makes the app's connection target-agnostic; it must actually be used
An app pointed at the original server name bypasses the listener and won't follow a failover
Writes to the old primary after failover should fail (it's now read-only), which is the diagnostic giveaway
The fix requires updating the connection string and then re-verifying with another test

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the connection string bypassing the listener endpoint as the cause
Correctly explains why writes to the old primary should fail, not silently succeed
Proposes the correct fix (use the listener endpoint)
Recommends re-testing after the fix rather than assuming it worked

questions.title: A Report Is Hung Behind an Open Transaction
questions.prompt: A user reports that a report query has been 'spinning' for ten minutes. You check sys.dm_exec_requests and find it's blocked by a session that shows status 'sleeping' with an open_tran count of 1 and no currently executing request. Explain what's happening and the two different ways you could resolve it right now.
questions.modelAnswer: A session can hold locks and show status 'sleeping' at the same time -- sleeping only means it's not currently executing a batch, not that it released anything. The open_tran count of 1 confirms it has an uncommitted transaction sitting open, most likely because an application or an ad-hoc SSMS session ran BEGIN TRANSACTION, made a change, and then simply stopped -- maybe the developer walked away, or the client disconnected without the driver closing the transaction cleanly. Every lock that transaction acquired is still held, which is exactly what's blocking the report's SELECT. There are two realistic ways to resolve it immediately: first, if you can identify who owns the session (via sys.dm_exec_sessions' login_name, host_name, and program_name) and they're reachable, ask them to COMMIT or ROLLBACK it themselves, which is the cleanest resolution since you're not guessing what they intended; second, if they're unreachable or it's clearly an abandoned connection, KILL the session ID directly, which forces SQL Server to roll back whatever was open and release its locks, unblocking the report immediately. Either way, the follow-up is finding out why an application or script left a transaction open without committing it, since this will keep recurring until that's fixed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that trips people up here is 'sleeping' -- a lot of people assume sleeping means idle and harmless, but it just means the session isn't actively running a batch right now; it can still be sitting on an open transaction holding every lock it already acquired. open_tran = 1 confirms that's exactly what's happening -- somebody started a transaction and never finished it, probably because they ran BEGIN TRANSACTION in SSMS to test something and got pulled away, or an application connection died without the transaction being cleanly closed. In the moment, I have two real options. If I can see who it is from sys.dm_exec_sessions -- login name, host, program name -- and I can reach them, I'll ask them to commit or roll back themselves, because they know what that transaction was actually doing and I don't want to guess. If it's clearly dead -- an old SSMS tab nobody's touched in twenty minutes, or a disconnected app session -- I'll just KILL the session ID, which rolls it back and frees the locks immediately. Either way, I'm flagging it afterward: an open transaction left dangling isn't a one-off annoyance, it's a sign something -- a script, a connection pool setting, an app bug -- isn't closing its transactions properly, and that's worth actually chasing down.
commonMistakes: Assuming a 'sleeping' status means the session can't be holding locks or blocking anyone
Immediately killing the session without first checking whether its owner is reachable and could safely commit or roll back themselves
Not checking open_tran count, and misdiagnosing the blocking as a long-running query instead of an abandoned transaction
Fixing the immediate block without investigating why the transaction was left open in the first place
keyPoints: A 'sleeping' session can still hold locks from an open transaction
open_tran > 0 with no active request indicates an abandoned or forgotten transaction
Identifying the session owner and asking them to commit/rollback is the cleanest fix when possible
KILLing the session forces a rollback and releases locks when the owner is unreachable

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that a sleeping session can still hold locks via an open transaction
Correctly diagnoses the open_tran count as the root cause
Describes both resolution options (owner commits/rollbacks, or KILL)
Mentions following up on the underlying cause

questions.title: A MongoDB Query That Suddenly Got Slow
questions.prompt: A MongoDB query that used to return in milliseconds is now taking several seconds as a collection has grown. Walk through how you'd use explain() to confirm the cause, and what you'd expect to see change in the output once you add the right index.
questions.modelAnswer: Running db.collection.find({...}).explain('executionStats') returns a winningPlan tree along with executionStats -- the two fields to check first are totalDocsExamined and totalKeysExamined compared against nReturned. If totalDocsExamined is close to the entire collection's document count while nReturned is small, the winningPlan stage will show a COLLSCAN -- a full collection scan -- confirming MongoDB is reading every document and filtering in memory rather than using an index, which is exactly what gets slower as the collection grows since there's more to scan every time. After creating an index on the query's filter field(s) and re-running the same explain(), you'd expect the winningPlan stage to change from COLLSCAN to IXSCAN, and totalDocsExamined should drop dramatically, now closely tracking nReturned instead of the whole collection -- MongoDB is navigating directly to matching documents via the index rather than reading past every non-matching one. executionTimeMillis in the output gives a direct before/after number to confirm the fix actually worked, not just that the plan looks different.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is always explain('executionStats'), not just explain() with no argument, because the default mode only shows the plan MongoDB would choose, not what actually happened when it ran. The two numbers I go straight to are totalDocsExamined and nReturned -- if totalDocsExamined is in the hundreds of thousands and nReturned is twelve, that's the whole story right there: MongoDB is reading nearly the entire collection into memory and throwing most of it away, and the winningPlan.stage will confirm it with COLLSCAN. That also explains why it used to be fast and isn't anymore -- a collection scan's cost scales directly with collection size, so as the collection grew, the exact same query got linearly slower with no code change needed to cause it. Once I add an index on the fields actually being filtered on and re-run the identical explain(), I expect to see the stage flip to IXSCAN and totalDocsExamined collapse down to roughly match nReturned, because now it's navigating straight to the matching documents instead of reading past everything else. I always compare executionTimeMillis before and after too, since that's the number that actually matters to whoever reported the slowness.
commonMistakes: Running explain() with no mode argument and only looking at the proposed plan, not actual execution stats
Not comparing totalDocsExamined against nReturned, missing the clearest signal of an unindexed scan
Creating an index on the wrong field, then being confused when the stage is still COLLSCAN
Assuming a slow query is a MongoDB problem in general rather than a missing-index problem specific to this query shape
keyPoints: explain('executionStats') shows what actually happened, not just the proposed plan
totalDocsExamined far exceeding nReturned signals an unindexed or poorly indexed query
winningPlan.stage of COLLSCAN confirms a full collection scan
A correctly targeted index flips the stage to IXSCAN and collapses totalDocsExamined toward nReturned

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses explain('executionStats') rather than the default explain mode
Correctly identifies totalDocsExamined vs. nReturned as the key diagnostic
Correctly identifies COLLSCAN as the root-cause signal
Correctly describes the expected before/after change after indexing

questions.title: Choosing a clustering key for a new fact-staging table
questions.prompt: You're designing a new staging table that will be loaded nightly and queried immediately afterward by ProductID ranges. A table can have only one clustered index. Explain the difference between a clustered and nonclustered index, and what makes a good choice of clustering key.
questions.modelAnswer: A clustered index determines the actual physical order rows are stored in on disk -- which is exactly why a table can have only one: data can only be physically sorted one way. A nonclustered index is a separate structure that holds a sorted copy of the indexed column(s) plus a pointer back to the actual row, and a table can have many of them. Looking up a row through the clustering key is fastest, since SQL Server navigates directly to the physical location; looking up through a nonclustered index takes one extra step -- find the index entry, then follow the pointer back to the row. A good clustering key is narrow (a small data type, since every nonclustered index secretly stores the clustering key as its row pointer), unique (no ambiguity about physical order), and ever-increasing (so new rows append at the end instead of forcing existing rows to physically shuffle). Given the staging table is loaded nightly and then range-queried by ProductID, an ever-increasing identity key for the clustered index, with a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries, is the more defensible design than clustering directly on ProductID.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as two separate decisions. First: what should the table's physical row order be -- that's the clustered index, and I only get one shot at it. Second: what other lookup patterns do I need to support cheaply -- that's where nonclustered indexes come in, and I can have several. For a staging table that's loaded nightly, I actually lean toward an ever-increasing identity column as the clustering key rather than ProductID directly, even though ProductID is the column people will query by. The reason is load performance: an ever-increasing key means new rows always append at the end of the physical order, so the nightly load doesn't cause page splits from inserting into the middle of existing data. Then I add a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries -- yes, that costs one extra pointer-following step per lookup compared to clustering directly on ProductID, but it's a much smaller cost than the load-time page-splitting I'd get from clustering on a column that isn't naturally ordered or unique.
commonMistakes: Assuming more indexes are always better without considering the nightly load's insert cost
Choosing a wide, non-unique column as the clustering key, which bloats every nonclustered index that secretly carries it as a pointer
Forgetting a table can have only one clustered index, and trying to 'cluster' on two different columns
Not connecting the ever-increasing key recommendation to the specific nightly-load write pattern described in the scenario
keyPoints: Clustered index = physical row order, one per table
Nonclustered index = separate structure with a pointer back to the row, many allowed
Good clustering key: narrow, unique, ever-increasing
Design choice should weigh load (insert) pattern against query (read) pattern

questions.title: Choosing Between Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, and a VM
questions.prompt: A company is migrating 40 databases from an on-prem SQL Server farm. Fifteen of them are small, independent application databases with no cross-database dependencies. The other 25 are heavily interconnected, rely on SQL Agent jobs, linked servers, and frequent cross-database queries, and the team doesn't want to rewrite any application code. Propose an architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: This genuinely calls for a mixed architecture rather than forcing all 40 databases onto one tier. The 15 independent databases, with no cross-database dependencies, are a clean fit for Azure SQL Database -- likely grouped into one or more elastic pools if their usage patterns are bursty and don't all peak simultaneously, which shares compute across them more cost-effectively than provisioning each one individually. The 25 interconnected databases are a clear fit for Azure SQL Managed Instance instead, specifically because the requirement list -- cross-database queries, linked servers, SQL Agent jobs, and zero appetite for rewriting application code -- maps almost exactly onto the set of instance-level features Managed Instance was built to preserve, while still being PaaS, meaning Microsoft still patches the OS and database engine. Choosing Azure SQL Database for those 25 would force breaking cross-database queries and finding workarounds for SQL Agent and linked servers, which directly contradicts the stated constraint of not rewriting application code. The tradeoff to flag honestly: running two different service tiers means two different operational models and cost structures to manage, but that's a smaller cost than forcing 25 genuinely interconnected databases into a tier that doesn't support how they actually work.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't force this onto one tier, because the two groups genuinely have different requirements, and trying to make one size fit both means compromising on at least one group. The 15 independent databases are the easy half -- Azure SQL Database, probably pooled into one or more elastic pools if their load patterns don't all spike together, since that's the more cost-efficient way to host a bunch of smaller, individually-light databases. The 25 interconnected ones are where the requirements actually decide the architecture for me: cross-database queries, linked servers, and SQL Agent jobs are specifically the instance-level features Azure SQL Database doesn't fully support, and the team has explicitly said no application rewrites are on the table. That rules out Database tier for this group and points straight at Managed Instance, which was built to preserve almost all of that instance-level behavior while still being a managed PaaS offering. I'd be upfront that running two tiers side by side means two things to operationally manage instead of one, but that's a much smaller cost than trying to retrofit 25 genuinely interdependent databases into a tier that was never designed to support how they actually work together.
commonMistakes: Forcing all 40 databases onto a single tier for operational simplicity, ignoring the real functional requirements of the interconnected group
Choosing Azure SQL Database for the interconnected 25 without recognizing it doesn't support cross-database queries the way the application needs
Not considering elastic pools for the 15 independent databases, missing a real cost-efficiency opportunity
Dismissing Managed Instance as 'too expensive' without weighing the cost of rewriting application code instead
keyPoints: A mixed architecture using both Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance fits two genuinely different requirement sets
Managed Instance is the right fit for databases needing cross-database queries, linked servers, and SQL Agent without code changes
Elastic pools suit multiple smaller, independent databases with non-simultaneous usage peaks
Operating two tiers side by side is a real cost, but smaller than forcing incompatible requirements onto one tier

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a mixed architecture rather than forcing one tier for all 40 databases
Correctly matches Managed Instance's features to the interconnected group's stated requirements
Correctly proposes elastic pools for the independent group
Honestly acknowledges the operational tradeoff of running two tiers

questions.title: Designing HA/DR Around a Stated RPO and RTO
questions.prompt: Finance tells you their reporting database can tolerate being down for up to 4 hours (RTO), but can't lose more than 5 minutes of data (RPO) in a regional outage. Propose a concrete Azure SQL HA/DR design that satisfies both numbers, and explain what would have to change if the RPO requirement tightened to near-zero.
questions.modelAnswer: An RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 4 hours are both comfortably achievable with an Auto-Failover Group using asynchronous geo-replication to a secondary region -- asynchronous replication typically has a replication lag in the range of seconds, well under the 5-minute RPO budget, and a failover group's automatic failover (or even a manual one, given a 4-hour RTO budget) comfortably fits within the time allowed. Within the primary region, zone-redundant or geo-zone-redundant backup storage and the database's built-in high-availability architecture (which already handles most single-node failures transparently) cover the more common, smaller-scale outage without needing a full regional failover at all. If the RPO requirement tightened to near-zero -- meaning essentially no data loss is acceptable in a regional outage -- asynchronous replication's inherent lag (even if usually small) is no longer provably safe, and the design would need to move toward synchronous replication, which guarantees zero data loss but at the cost of added write latency, since every write now has to be confirmed by the secondary before it's acknowledged as committed -- a cost that's often only accepted for the most critical systems given what it does to write performance, especially across any real geographic distance.
questions.professionalAnswer: For 5 minutes RPO and 4 hours RTO, I wouldn't reach for anything exotic -- an Auto-Failover Group with standard asynchronous geo-replication to a secondary region comfortably satisfies both. Asynchronous replication's lag is typically seconds, so 5 minutes of tolerated data loss gives real headroom, and 4 hours of tolerated downtime is more than enough time for either automatic or even manual failover to complete. For the more common case of a localized failure rather than a full regional outage, the database's built-in HA architecture and zone-redundant backups already handle that without needing to touch the DR failover at all. Where this gets genuinely harder is if someone later comes back and says the RPO needs to be near-zero -- that's a different conversation entirely, because asynchronous replication, by definition, has some lag, however small, and 'near-zero data loss' means I can no longer treat that lag as negligible. At that point the design has to move to synchronous replication, which guarantees no data loss by holding up every write until the secondary confirms it -- but that adds real latency to every single write, scaled by the distance between regions, and that's a cost I'd want finance to understand concretely before committing to it, because 'near-zero RPO' sounds like a small ask until you see what it does to write performance.
commonMistakes: Over-engineering with synchronous replication for a 5-minute RPO that asynchronous replication already satisfies comfortably
Not distinguishing a localized, in-region failure (handled by built-in HA) from a full regional outage (handled by geo-replication/failover groups)
Assuming RPO and RTO are the same concept, or using them interchangeably in the design explanation
Not flagging the real write-latency cost of synchronous replication when the RPO requirement tightens
keyPoints: Asynchronous geo-replication via an Auto-Failover Group comfortably satisfies a 5-minute RPO / 4-hour RTO
Built-in HA and zone-redundant backups handle smaller, in-region failures without a full regional failover
A near-zero RPO requirement requires synchronous replication instead of asynchronous
Synchronous replication guarantees zero data loss at the cost of added write latency

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a correctly-scoped design (failover group, async replication) for the stated RPO/RTO
Correctly distinguishes in-region HA from cross-region DR in the design
Correctly explains what changes (synchronous replication) if RPO tightens to near-zero
Explains the real latency tradeoff of synchronous replication
